See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
Rabobank made no profit growth in the first half of this year, reporting a net profit of nearly €2.7 billion, the same as in the first six months of 2025, after setting aside €562 million for loans that might not be repaid.
That is more than four times the €136 million it set aside a year earlier, the bank said in its results statement.
Chairman Stefaan Decraene told reporters the provisions related to two cases in South America but declined to name the companies or projects involved, broadcaster NOS reported.
Business in the Netherlands grew. Deposits at the Dutch retail arm stood at €375.1 billion, and lending at €293 billion.
Takeover talk

Rabobank also said it will invest up to €2 billion in strengthening its data and IT systems and scaling up its use of artificial intelligence. Reuters reported that the spending will be spread over the next three years.
The bank’s return on equity was 9.5% and its core capital ratio 20.2%, which it said makes it one of the best-capitalised banks in Europe.

Man who held prison staff hostage given suspended jail sentence
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
A man who held three prison staff hostage at knifepoint for several hours has been given a further suspended sentence of a year.
Corné H. seized and handcuffed his victims for several hours on December 5 last year at the jail in Vught after threatening them and five other colleagues with kitchen knives.
The 30-year-old had served a nine-month term for holding four staff at a bar in Ede, Gelderland, against their will in March the previous year.
At the time of the incident he was being detained in Vught’s psychiatric unit waiting to be given a place in a clinic under the Dutch compulsory treatment system (tbs).
The sentence was suspended to allow H. to continue his treatment, which began in June, meaning he will only have to go back to prison if he commits another offence.
The court in Den Bosch heard that H. suffered as a result of conditions including PTSS, schizophrenia and autism, which influenced his behaviour. A psychiatric assessment also said he had “anti-social and borderline personality traits”.
The judge said his victims feared for their lives and the incident “must have been dreadful for them”, but accepted H. had diminished responsibility and imposed a sentence that met the prosecution service’s demands.
At the earlier trial, H. was cleared of taking the bar staff in Ede hostage but convicted of depriving them of their liberty and threatening them.
Police sealed off the venue after he went in at closing time with guns and explosives and threatened to blow up the building, leading to a stand-off lasting more than eight hours.

items.title: Police raise concerns over sharp rise in weapon seizures
items.summary: Dutch police seized 5,165 gas and alarm pistols, air weapons and pepper sprays last year, up from 4,080 in 2022,...
items.body_text:
Police raise concerns over sharp rise in weapon seizures
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
Dutch police seized 5,165 gas and alarm pistols, air weapons and pepper sprays last year, up from 4,080 in 2022, according to figures given to broadcaster NOS – a rise of almost 27%.
Police said they did not know whether the increase indicates that more people are carrying such weapons, or if it reflects boosted efforts to find and confiscate them.
Gas and alarm pistols are the main worry because they are hard to tell apart from real firearms, police spokesman Martin van der Meij told NOS. Alarm pistols make a loud bang but fire no projectile, while gas weapons can release tear gas.
They are cheap, easy to obtain and relatively simple to convert into working firearms, he said. A converted pistol was used to kill the crime reporter Peter R. de Vries in 2021.
Buying these weapons in Germany or Belgium and bringing them into the Netherlands is a criminal offence, though people do not always realise it.
Herman Oldenkotte, who runs a gun shop in Gronau just over the German border from Enschede, told NOS that he estimated 80% to 90% of his customers were Dutch. In Germany the weapons can be bought without a licence by anyone over 18.
Police also say more weapons are arriving by post. The Netherlands has pressed the EU for years to bring in a licence requirement or a ban.
Pepper spray is banned for civilians under Dutch weapons law. The justice ministry said in June it planned to allow permits for people at particular risk, such as stalking victims, while ruling out legalising it for everyone.

items.title: Pole becomes first person to swim 160km Baltic Sea route between Sweden and Poland
items.summary: Bartłomiej Kubkowski managed the crossing at his fifth attempt, raising hundreds of thousands for charity.
items.body_text:
Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work!
Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support.
Polish swimmer Bartłomiej Kubkowski has become the first person in history to swim across the Baltic Sea between Sweden and Poland, covering a distance of just over 160 kilometres (99 miles).
On Sunday evening, an exhausted Kubkowski clambered onto the beach in the town of Dziwnów on Poland’s northern Baltic coast, around 56 hours after he had set off from Kaseberga in Sweden on Friday.
The achievement marks a personal triumph for Kubkowski, for whom this was the fifth attempt to complete the route. His effort this year has raised over 715,000 zloty (€166,000) for children’s cancer treatment so far, with donations to his fundraiser still coming in.
View this post on Instagram
During the crossing, Kubkowski was unable to sleep and, although a support boat accompanied him and provided food and drink, he was not allowed to touch the vessel itself.
His journey of around 160km was not far off the longest-ever continuous, unassisted open-water swim ratified by the Marathon Swimmers Federation, which was the 168.3 km swum by American Sarah Thomas in 2017 in Lake Champlain, between the US states of New York and Vermont.
Kubkowski has been attempting to swim the route between Sweden and Poland since 2022, getting progressively closer to achieving the goal. Last year, he came within 11km of the Polish coast before extreme exhaustion and deteriorating weather forced him to give up, reported Eurosport.
However, Kubkowski, a former competitive swimmer who now devotes himself to ultraswimming, did last year manage to break the world record for the longest distance swum in a swimming pool over 24 hours, after he managed to cover 103.6 km (64.5 miles).
Another Polish swimmer, Karolina Szczepaniak, is also currently attempting to swim from Sweden to Poland along a slightly different route to Kubkowski’s. At the time of writing, she is around 110km into the 172km journey, and has raised almost 400,000 zloty for charity.
Szczepaniak, a former Olympic swimmer, also attempted the feat last year, but was forced to give up after 57 hours amid worsening weather.
However, the 146.7km she swam set a new record for the longest distance covered by a female swimmer in the Baltic Sea and a Polish record for open-water swimming by a woman.

Daniel Tilles is editor-in-chief of Notes from Poland. He has written on Polish affairs for a wide range of publications, including Foreign Policy, POLITICO Europe, EUobserver and Dziennik Gazeta Prawna.

items.title: Canadian company launches €7.5bn bid for Polish convenience store chain Żabka
items.summary: The convenience store operator Alimentation Couche-Tard has already secured majority shareholder support.
items.body_text:
Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work!
Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support.
A Canadian multinational operator of convenience stores, Alimentation Couche-Tard, has announced plans to acquire Poland’s Żabka Group, which runs Europe’s largest chain of convenience stores.
The company has offered 32 zloty per share, valuing Żabka at 32.6 billion zloty (€7.56 billion). Żabka’s main shareholders have agreed to sell their stakes, with final approval still required from stock market investors.
If the transaction is completed, Żabka is likely to be delisted from the Warsaw Stock Exchange just two years after its market debut.
Właściciel Circle K chce przejąć 100% Żabki. Cena w wezwaniu ma wynieść 32 zł za akcję
via @PawelBiedrzycki https://t.co/61XEGuQnnB
— Strefa Inwestorów (@strefainw) July 31, 2026
The acquisition will be carried out through Alimentation Couche-Tard’s Polish subsidiary, Circle K, which runs petrol stations, and will cover all of Żabka Group’s more than one million shares.
Alimentation Couche-Tard has already secured commitments to acquire at least 57.2% of the company. Heket, an entity linked to CVC Capital Partners owning 37.6% of Żabka’s shares, and PG Investment Company, holding 10%, have agreed to sell their entire stakes.
A group of major individual shareholders, together controlling 9.6% of Żabka’s shares, has also agreed to sell its holdings to the Canadian buyer. The investors include members of the company’s management and former executives.
They have also agreed to reinvest part of the proceeds from the sale into Alimentation Couche-Tard shares.
The tender offer for the remaining shares was announced on Friday by Ipopema Securities, which is acting as the intermediary in the transaction.
Alimentation Couche-Tard and Żabka expect subscriptions for the offer to open around 26 August, following a review of the tender document by the Polish Financial Supervision Authority (KNF). The companies foresee the transaction closing by the end of the year.
The Canadian company expects Żabka to continue operating independently, under the leadership of its current management team, and to retain its brand.
Żabka shares jumped after the announcement, rising from 29.26 zloty to around 31.60 zloty on Friday afternoon, an increase of about 8%.
Żabka, which runs Europe’s largest chain of convenience stores, has made its stock market debut in one of Europe’s biggest listings this year.
Its IPO was the fourth largest in the history of the Warsaw Stock Exchange and valued the firm at €5 billion https://t.co/fmqLteZjdR
— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 18, 2024
If completed, the acquisition would be the largest takeover in the history of Alimentation Couche-Tard, which already owns 17,300 stores across 27 countries.
Alex Miller, Alimentation Couche-Tard’s CEO, said the company is “committed to supporting the continued growth of the Żabka business while drawing from its strengths in areas such as food, digital engagement, customer loyalty, private brand, supply chain, logistics and innovation”.
Żabka made its debut on the Warsaw Stock Exchange in 2024 in one of Europe’s largest initial public offerings that year, with a valuation of around €5 billion.
The company is Poland’s largest convenience store operator, with about 13,000 locations nationwide run by around 11,000 franchisees. It has also expanded internationally, opening its first stores in Romania and reaching 100 outlets there last year.
Poland’s largest convenience chain, Żabka, has opened the 100th store of its Romanian brand, Froo, one year after launching there.
“We are learning from local consumers and laying the groundwork for a long-term presence in Romania,” says Żabka’s VP.https://t.co/0CaZTaVhlB

items.title: The split in Poland’s opposition could help them unseat Tusk’s government [Opinion]
items.summary: Daniel Tilles It may help broaden the opposition's appeal by offering voters a more moderate, centre-right option.
items.body_text:
Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work!
Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support.
By Daniel Tilles
If Mateusz Morawiecki cuts his final ties with PiS and forms a new party, it may help broaden the opposition’s appeal by offering voters a more moderate, centre-right option.
While the strings have not yet been fully cut, Poland’s main opposition party, the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS), is splitting in two.
A group of 40 MPs led by former Prime Minister (and PiS deputy leader) Mateusz Morawiecki have now formed a separate parliamentary caucus of their own, after last week refusing to sign a pledge of loyalty and quit the association they had formed – as had been demanded by PiS leader Jarosław Kaczyński.
Former Polish PM @MorawieckiM says 41 lawmakers aligned with him will form their own parliamentary caucus, deepening a split in conservative opposition party @pisorgpl.
The proposed group would become the third-largest bloc in Poland's Sejmhttps://t.co/coOdpS7pia
— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 29, 2026
The move means that Morawiecki’s caucus, known as Development Plus (Rozwój Plus), is now the third largest in parliament, while PiS, which is down to 147 MPs, has lost its status as the biggest.
For now, most of Morawiecki’s followers officially remain members of the PiS party, a situation that will only change if they either resign or are thrown out following a disciplinary process that could take weeks.
But unless either or both sides make major concessions, it seems only a matter of time before Development Plus becomes a separate party.
A lot of international reporting has suggested that these developments will harm Poland’s right-wing opposition and boost the re-election chances of Prime Minister Donald Tusk’s more liberal coalition at next year’s parliamentary elections. In fact, PiS’s split could well help the opposition win a majority.
Over the last year, PiS has found itself in an increasingly difficult position. Its support in the polls has fallen below 25%, the party’s lowest level in 14 years. Meanwhile, combined support for two far-right opposition groups – Confederation (Konfederacja) and Confederation of the Polish Crown (KKP) – has risen to over 20%, threatening PiS’s longstanding dominance on the right.
In response, Kaczyński has pushed his party in a more rightward direction, picking a hardline figure, Przemysław Czarnek, as PiS’s prime ministerial candidate in March.
That signalled that PiS was aiming to compete head to head with the far right on many issues, taking tougher positions on Ukraine, the EU, migration and climate policy. In many cases, that meant disowning the legacy of the PiS government led by Morawiecki from 2017 to 2023.
It also meant that the party was ceding the centre ground, something Morawiecki, who represents the more moderate, technocratic side of PiS, was particularly concerned about (alongside his own waning influence).
When in power, PiS launched a revolution in Poland's energy transition. But now, in opposition, it has disowned those achievements and returned to an emphasis on coal.
This could be a missed opportunity to win back centrist voters, writes @OrzelBartlomiej https://t.co/8cGvubn7N2
— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 29, 2026
Should Morawiecki now, as expected, launch his own centre-right party, focused on economic development, it would appeal to moderate conservatives who are opposed to the Tusk government but put off by the far right and PiS’s own hardline turn.
Inevitably, some of the support for Development Plus would come at the expense of PiS – but not all of it, and possibly not even most of it. An example of something similar happening can be seen elsewhere among the opposition.
Until last year, KKP was part of Confederation

items.title: Tallinn's beloved Old Thomas symbol takes center stage in Sõru Museum exhibit
items.summary: At the Sõru Museum on Hiiumaa, it is possible to explore items bearing the motif of Tallinn's symbol — the weather vane Old Thomas — from the private collection of Eero Kööp.
items.body_text:
Tallinn's beloved Old Thomas symbol takes center stage in Sõru Museum exhibit
At the Sõru Museum on Hiiumaa, it is possible to explore items bearing the motif of Tallinn's symbol — the weather vane Old Thomas — from the private collection of Eero Kööp.
At the Sõru Museum, Old Thomas is depicted on very different kinds of objects. Collector Eero Kööp said he has found, bought and received these items as gifts over roughly ten years.
"I don't remember how the interest started. Maybe it began with one wall plaque. Many items were left out of this exhibition," Kööp said.
Tallinn's guardian Old Thomas, or Vana Toomas in Estonian, will soon be celebrating a major anniversary.
"The Old Thomas weather vane was placed on the [Tallinn Town Hall] tower when the year was 1530. But according to one legend, he was named Thomas later," Kööp said.
It is also unknown who the author of the first Old Thomas — now held at the Tallinn City Museum — originally was. And in broad terms, Old Thomas has retained his appearance over five centuries.
"But he has been stylized in several different ways. For example, once we had a sister city, Schwerin, and they made him into a complete clown. At the request of restaurants, Old Thomas looks a bit different. But mostly he is still the same — the flag is always on one side," Kööp said.
Most of the Old Thomas items on display at the exhibition date back decades. The best‑known object is perhaps the former Estoplast factory's Old Thomas table lamp from the Soviet era. But today's so‑called modern Old Thomases have a completely different story.
"Modern Old Thomases are made in China. Our souvenir sellers order their products from China," Kööp noted.
And the reason such an exhibition was set up on Hiiumaa at all is very simple and practical.
"Here at the Sõru end, Eero Kööp had a few Old Thomases, and over ten years he collected more. Then the time came when he needed to do renovations at home. And then he came to the museum and asked whether an exhibition could be made. And that's how it started to branch out," said Sõru Museum director Eve Ellermäe.
--
Editor: Marko Tooming, Argo Ideon

items.title: Estonia's new ambassadors take up their posts
items.summary: At the beginning of August, several Estonian ambassadors to foreign countries took up new postings, including the ambassadors to the United States, Canada and NATO.
items.body_text:
Estonia's new ambassadors take up their posts
At the beginning of August, several Estonian ambassadors to foreign countries took up new postings, including the ambassadors to the United States, Canada and NATO.
Hannes Hanso succeeded Kristjan Prikk as Estonia's ambassador to the United States, based in Washington. Since 2022, Hanso had served as Estonia's ambassador to China, as well as to Vietnam, Mongolia and Thailand.
Prikk, who had served as Estonia's ambassador to the United States since 2021, in turn succeeded Jüri Luik as Estonia's permanent representative to NATO.
Marje Luup was appointed Estonia's ambassador to Kazakhstan, based in Astana.
Estonia's previous ambassador to Kazakhstan, Jaap Ora, resigned on December 9 last year after drawing criticism from Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna (Eesti 200) and Foreign Ministry Secretary General Jonatan Vseviov over President Alar Karis' state visit to Kazakhstan. Ora has since challenged his dismissal in court.
Luup previously served as Estonia's ambassador to India, as well as to Bangladesh and Sri Lanka. She was succeeded in New Delhi in August by Kristi Karelsohn.
Ambassadors were also replaced in Canada, Ukraine, Albania, Hungary, Ireland, Spain, Portugal and Brazil.
Gert Auväärt succeeded Margus Rava as Estonia's ambassador to Canada, based in Ottawa.
Tiina Intelmann succeeded Annely Kolk as Estonia's ambassador to Ukraine, based in Kyiv.
Piret Urb succeeded Karin Rannu as Estonia's ambassador to Albania, based in Athens.
Jana Vanamölder succeeded Raul Toomas as Estonia's ambassador to Hungary, based in Budapest.
Kairi Saar-Isop succeeded Kairi Künka as Estonia's ambassador to Ireland, based in Dublin.
Lembit Uibo succeeded Andres Rundu as Estonia's ambassador to Spain, based in Madrid.
Katrin Kivi succeeded Moonika Kase as Estonia's ambassador to Portugal, based in Lisbon.
Estonia also opened new embassies this year in Yerevan, the capital of Armenia; Chișinău, the capital of Moldova; Baku, the capital of Azerbaijan; Brasília, the capital of Brazil; and Nairobi, the capital of Kenya.
Former Ambassador to Portugal Moonika Kase was appointed Estonia's first ambassador to Brazil, based in Brasília.
Tiina Nirk was appointed Estonia's ambassador to Azerbaijan, based in Baku.
Siiri Königsberg was appointed Estonia's ambassador to Moldova, based in Chișinău.
Several diplomatic rotations are still to come.
Daniel Erik Schaer will take up his post as Estonia's ambassador to Kenya, based in Nairobi, on August 31.
Estonia's ambassador to Latvia, based in Riga, will change on December 1, when Celia Kuningas-Saagpakk succeeds Eerik Marmei.
Kuningas-Saagpakk had previously served as Estonia's ambassador to the Holy See, based in Tallinn. She was succeeded by Minna-Liina Lind.
--
Editor: Valner Väino, Marcus Turovski

items.title: Estonia ramps up defenses against invasive pests as warming climate hikes risks
items.summary: A combination of a warming climate and international trade and mobility have meant invasive species and threats once unheard of in Estonia are now threatening to arrive here.
items.body_text:
Estonia ramps up defenses against invasive pests as warming climate hikes risks
A combination of a warming climate and international trade and mobility have meant invasive species and threats once unheard of in Estonia are now threatening to arrive here.
From plant-eating, flying beetles, to parasites which themselves attach to beetles and other bugs, to those species which can affect wooden items, such as pallets, there is a range of potential pests which could devastate Estonia's forests and gardens.
This would be particularly poignant given Estonia has for over 20 years held the EU's rare protected zone status, which means strict restrictions on plants entering the country from other EU member states and the use of "plant passports."
Alien species rarely reach Estonia of their own accord. Instead, they arrive with the aid of human activity. Global supply chains, timber imports and busy international travel all provide ideal pathways for insects and plant diseases to spread. The authorities' watchlist now has nearly 500 different threats.
Speaking to radio program "Ökoskoop," Ülle Metsmann, plant health adviser at the state Agriculture and Food Board (PTA), stressed how critical prevention is, starting at Estonia's borders.
"One of the most important plant health measures is barring new pests from reaching Estonia via trade. Border crossing areas are naturally high-risk locations for surveillance, where it would make sense to set traps and monitor trees and shrubs," she said.
Changing weather conditions have also been leading to an expansion of the workload facing customs inspectors, and also plant health inspectors, particularly the milder winters and longer warm periods, which have allowed species from more southerly climes to survive more easily than they could previously.
As a result, many pests and bacteria that would have perished during the Estonian winter are increasingly successfully overwintering, for instance in the Estonian soil or beneath tree bark.
"Climate change is definitely affecting the spread of plant pests as a warmer climate favors their survival. The warmer it gets, the more suitable the conditions get for species that have not previously established themselves here," Metsmann noted.
One of the greatest concerns has been the emerald ash borer, a beetle native to northeastern China which is responsible for the rapid destruction of native ash trees. It has not been found in Estonia yet, but it is making steady progress into the EU more broadly.
After getting established in Ukraine some years ago, this tiny species of beetle somewhat unexpectedly began moving further towards Central Europe, and has now also been detected in the EU nations of Hungary and Slovakia.
"Given the current situation, you can imagine how little capacity Ukraine's national plant protection service has to monitor this pest. Unfortunately, it has now reached the European Union, which means a great deal of additional work for the countries where it has been found," the adviser said.
In addition to the bug being found to Estonia's south, it has also turned up to the east as well, and close to Estonia. Four years ago, a viable population of the pest was discovered near St. Petersburg, just 150 kilometers from the Estonian border, putting local specialists on high alert.
As a beetle, the species can fly too, of course. "It is an insect with excellent flying ability, so its arrival here from the St. Petersburg area is highly likely. At some point it will make that journey. Our task is to detect it as early as possible so we are prepared," Metsmann explained.
The emerald ash borer measures just 1.4 centimeters in length, maximum, so is extremely difficult to spot in the wild with the naked eye. To improve early detection, the state maintains 90 special sticky traps along the eastern border and along major highways, replacing them every couple of weeks.

items.title: North Macedonia Opposition Blasts ‘Secret Talks’ on Deal With Bulgaria
items.summary: Opposition condemns lack of transparency after Foreign Minister reveals government is working behind closed doors to solve dispute with Bulgaria and unblock EU talks.
items.body_text:
North Macedonia Opposition Blasts ‘Secret Talks’ on Deal With Bulgaria
North Macedonia’s Foreign Minister Timco Mucunski. Photo: North Macedonia’s MFA.
North Macedonia’s main opposition party, the Social Democrats, SDSM, accused Foreign Minister Timco Mucunski on Tuesday of holding “secret talks” about the country’s EU future behind the backs of its citizens.
“There is no normal country where a foreign minister says talks on the future of the country are a secret for its citizens,” the SDSM said.
The party accused the centre-right VMRO DPMNE-led government of Prime Minister Hristijan Mickoski of refusing to disclose details of important alleged negotiations.
The accusations came a day after Mucunski, in an interview with the state news agency MIA, said for the first time that the government was pursuing confidential efforts to find a “lasting and sustainable solution” to the long-running dispute with Bulgaria that has blocked the opening of EU accession talks.
“We are working on a solution, but not a solution at any cost, and not one that would prove unsustainable and bring us back to the situation we are in today,” Mucunski said, adding that revealing details could jeopardise the negotiations.
According to Mucunski, Skopje will not cross established “red lines” in these talks and is seeking guarantees from EU member states that its accession process will become more predictable once the current impasse is resolved.
Although he declined to identify those involved in the contacts, Mucunski suggested discussions were also taking place with several European partners behind closed doors in an attempt to break the years of deadlock.
North Macedonia’s accession talks have repeatedly stalled despite the country becoming an EU candidate back in 2005. After resolving a long-running dispute over its name with Greece, Skopje expected to move swiftly toward membership negotiations.
Instead, since 2020, Bulgaria blocked the process, arguing that North Macedonia had failed to address issues related to history, language and the rights of people who identify as Bulgarian.
An attempt to overcome the deadlock came in 2022 through the so-called French proposal, under which North Macedonia agreed to amend its constitution to include Bulgarians among its constitutionally recognised peoples.
However, the VMRO DPMNE-led government, which came to power in 2024, has stressed it will not act unless it receives guarantees that Bulgaria won’t block the country again, further down the line.
Mucunski’s remarks about quiet efforts to achieve a breakthrough come after the EU Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos last month called on North Macedonia again to change its constitution to speed up EU membership, making it clear that EU enlargement is not built on guarantees given in advance.

items.title: Election Race Starts As Bulgaria’s Acting President Seeks Full Mandate
items.summary: Iliana Iotova, a long-time socialist and previously a Vice-President to Rumen Radev, confirmed she will run in October’s presidential elections, as competitors emerge.
items.body_text:
Bulgaria’s acting President Iliana Iotova has confirmed she will be running in the upcoming presidential elections scheduled for October.
Iotova, who was previously a low-profile Vice-President to Rumen Radev, assumed office in January after Radev resigned in order to become Bulgaria’s Prime Minister. On July 28 the ruling party, Progressive Bulgaria, and the Bulgarian Socialist Party, where Iotova launched her career, officially endorsed her bid to become the permanent President. Two days later an opinion poll gave her a 50 per cent approval rating from members of the public, enough to give her a landslide win. Other opinion polls have indicated a high, but slightly decreased, support for Radev’s government.
“Iotova has quite a comfortable lead”, Zlatina Zehirova, internal politics editor at Dnevnik.bg, told BIRN. “There are about three months until the elections, in which Iotova's opponents will look for ways to make the most of the power imbalances.” Zehirova said Progressive Bulgaria’s support is both a blessing and a curse, because the shaky politics of Radev’s government might reflect negatively on Iotova's campaign.

items.title: When Propaganda Backfires: Lessons from Orban’s Social Media Defeat in Hungary Election
items.summary: Many factors contributed to the Hungarian government’s election defeat, including social media campaigns which misfired as public trust eroded. Yet Russian-style disinformation remains a persistent threat.
items.body_text:
It was clear from the heavy defeat of Viktor Orban’s government in April's election that its overwhelming dominance of Hungary’s media landscape wasn’t enough to get it across the line this time. Since then, emerging data shows just how ineffective the election campaign of the former Hungarian prime minister’s Fidesz party, its Christian-nationalist KDNP ally and its proxies really was.
According to the Vilnius-based narrative intelligence company Repsense, which combined three complementary analyses in the four months leading up to Hungary’s general election, several of the government’s efforts, including a false-flag operation involving an actual flag to discredit the opposition Tisza party, backfired badly.
As detailed in its non-public consolidated executive report seen by BIRN, Repsense tracked a total of 816,863 articles and posts across Hungarian-language news sites and Facebook, X, YouTube, TikTok, Instagram and Telegram between December 2025 and April 2026, containing 12.25 million unique sentences. (The company does not attempt to capture every account, but focuses its data collection on influential accounts and widely seen content across the political spectrum.)
The report shows that while content matching Fidesz campaign themes outweighed that matching opposition campaign themes by roughly four to one in volume, in several cases the counter-response travelled further and faster than the initial operation itself.
That doesn’t mean the propaganda of the former government didn't reach large numbers of Hungarians. After 16 years in power, Fidesz directly or indirectly controlled an estimated 80 per cent of Hungary's media landscape, spanning public and commercial broadcasters, national dailies, regional press and online outlets. The government's messaging was further reinforced by ubiquitous nationwide billboard campaigns. However, convincing their citizens proved a different story this time around.
Debunkings went more viral
A notable case was when several young people unfurled a huge Ukrainian flag at the Tisza party’s March 15 national holiday rally. Photos of the protest action were taken and rapidly spread by pro-Fidesz outlets and accounts, portraying the incident as evidence of the opposition party’s pro-Ukrainian alignment.
However, the independent outlet 444.hu quickly reported that the protest action had been coordinated by key staff members of a Fidesz-linked digital campaign agency. It also identified the two minors who had unfurled the flag, one of whom later that day posted an Instagram story showing him with the chairman of the Budapest organisation of Fidelitas, Fidesz’s youth wing.
Repsense examined the content database’s dimensions like viral intensity, which means how fast and how far a narrative spreads – a measure “driven mainly by posting speed (sentences per hour), acceleration, and how big the narrative got in its first six hours relative to its final size”. Regarding the flag issue, the original posts reached 28 points on their “Facebook deep-dive” analysis’ viral intensity scoring, while the exposure scored 44, achieving half of its total reach in under an hour – the fastest spread in their Facebook dataset.
“What the data shows is that Hungarian citizens used the same platforms not as passive consumers of propaganda, but as an active counter-disinformation force. This is a dynamic that echoes the earliest promise of social media as a tool for civic resistance, which brings back memories of the Arab Spring,” says Mykolas Katkus, co-founder and CEO of Repsense. “The information environment had developed an immune response – each new provocation only accelerated its own exposure.”

items.summary: Extremely low water levels in the Danube are keeping the Hungarian Defense Forces’ explosive ordnance disposal unit busy. At the same time, the dried-up riverbed is revealing fascinating insights into the Hungarian capital’s past. The ongoing heatwave is causing the Danube’s water level in the Budapest metropolitan area to drop steadily. While this poses an […] The post Record-Low Danube Water Levels Expose WWII Explosives and Historic Bridge Ruins appeared first on Hungary Today.
items.body_text:
The zoo uses habitat adaptations, cooling systems, special feeding methods, and increased hydration measures to help animals cope with rising temperatures.Continue reading
Extremely low water levels in the Danube are keeping the Hungarian Defense Forces’ explosive ordnance disposal unit busy. At the same time, the dried-up riverbed is revealing fascinating insights into the Hungarian capital’s past.
The ongoing heatwave is causing the Danube’s water level in the Budapest metropolitan area to drop steadily. While this poses an obstacle to shipping, it has sparked excitement among historians and is currently keeping the explosive ordnance disposal team working around the clock.
On the evening of August 2, dangerous remnants of the past came to light at the boat dock on Batthyány Square’s riverfront.
The falling water level revealed various explosive devices from World War II that had been hidden in the mud for decades.
Based on the statement from the Hungarian Defense Forces’ emergency response unit, special forces on the scene were able to identify and secure ten TMi-35 anti-tank mines, one hand grenade, and one kilogram of assorted infantry ammunition.
Just a few hundred meters away, near the Buda end of the Elisabeth Bridge, passersby also came across a significantly older artifact: a medieval cannonball. The discovery prompted a police operation on Sunday evening around 8:30 p.m. To ensure the bomb squad could safely remove the projectile, police closed the road to vehicle traffic for 500 meters northbound starting from the Buda end of the Elisabeth Bridge. Pedestrian traffic along the riverbank was also temporarily restricted. However, the Elisabeth Bridge itself did not need to be closed.
All recovered items were transported to the central collection point of the Hungarian Defense Forces.
In addition to the ammunition finds, the low water level is currently offering residents and tourists an extraordinary spectacle. The water is so shallow that from the present-day Liberty Bridge (Szabadság híd), one can see the bottom of the riverbed with the naked eye.
Walking from St. Gellért Square, the ruins of the historic Franz Joseph Bridge come into view at the first pier.
Inaugurated in 1896, the bridge was Budapest’s third road bridge. In January 1945—not even 50 years after its opening—it was blown up during World War II.
While most of the rubble on the Pest side was recovered after the war, the Buda half still lies at the bottom of the Danube to this day. The bridge was rebuilt as early as 1946 and reopened on August 20 under the name Liberty Bridge.
According to the weather service Időkép, the Danube has once again exposed these historical remains after eight years. The previous record low water level on the Budapest stretch of the Danube was set on October 25, 2018, when a level of just 33 centimeters was measured. That record was broken again last week—and since no significant rainfall is in sight for the time being, the Danube is likely to continue revealing its secrets for a little while longer.
Via MTI, időkép.hu; Featured photo: Facebook/Magyar Honvédség

items.title: Péter Magyar Ridiculed in Russian Media for his Attacks on Rosatom Amid the Ongoing Energy Crisis
items.summary: The river Danube is now reduced to a small stream near the Paks Nuclear Plant Péter Magyar’s pre- and post-election tirades against the cost of the modernization of Hungary’s Paks nuclear power plants, and his suggestions of an alleged plot by the former Orbán government to subordinate the country’s energy sovereignty to the Kremlin, […] The post Péter Magyar Ridiculed in Russian Media for his Attacks on Rosatom Amid the Ongoing Energy Crisis appeared first on Hungary Today.
items.body_text:
The plant provides nearly half of Hungary’s electricity generation.Continue reading
Péter Magyar’s pre- and post-election tirades against the cost of the modernization of Hungary’s Paks nuclear power plants, and his suggestions of an alleged plot by the former Orbán government to subordinate the country’s energy sovereignty to the Kremlin, are now coming under increasing scrutiny. Modernizing the Russian-built plant is very expensive indeed, but it is dwarfed by the consequences of not having it, writes the Russian outlet, Ria Novosti.
No sooner has Péter Magyar had a chance to fully savor his election victory than reality brought him crashing back down to earth. On his official page, the new Hungarian prime minister announced a declaration of a state of emergency in the energy sector, wrote the Russian news portal. The national operator MVM Paks Nuclear Power Station is about to shut down the country’s only nuclear power plant, and the decision is in no way related to scheduled preventive maintenance. Energy officials simply have no other choice, as the water level of the Danube—whose waters are used as a natural coolant—has dropped to critically low levels.
The shutdown of four VVER-440 reactors means that 2,000 megawatt-hours of electricity—or 40% of the country’s generation capacity—will be lost from the domestic grid. The head of state is urging his fellow citizens to voluntarily minimize consumption. The Hungarians are not alone in facing problems caused by the summer heatwave. The low water levels in the Danube forced Romania’s Nuclearelectrica to shut down the first power unit at the Cernavodă Nuclear Power Plant last Wednesday, and two days later, the second reactor suffered the same fate.
To understand the essence of what is happening, it should be noted that the core cooling systems of nuclear power plants can be configured in two ways, write Ria Novosti.
The simplest method is the direct flow method. Water from a river, lake, or the sea is piped to the turbine condensers, where it absorbs excess heat, and then, having been heated, is returned to the source. This method is the most reliable, but it requires a truly enormous amount of water. Depending on the turbines’ capacity, the flow rate can range from forty to one hundred cubic meters per second; accordingly, over 250 million cubic meters of water pass through the plant each month.
In areas where there are no major water sources but where the demand for electricity is high, power plants are cooled using recirculating systems with cooling towers. It is precisely these large, cone-shaped structures that are most often depicted in various photographs and posters symbolizing nuclear power. This method uses evaporative cooling, in which water circulates within a closed system, absorbing heat from the turbines and then cooling down again inside the cooling towers. This method is much more efficient, as only about two cubic meters of water per second are drawn from external sources, while approximately 60 million metric tons of water evaporate into the atmosphere each year.
The Danube’s annual runoff totals 6,400 cubic meters per second. This seems sufficient to meet the needs of the nuclear power industry, but it is not only the volume that matters here—temperature is also a key factor, and the water in Europe’s rivers has also warmed to record levels.
Conscientious citizen might now turn off all possible electrical appliances, but the residential sector accounts for about one-third of total consumption on average. The lion’s share comes from industrial facilities, which are either difficult or impossible to shut down partially or completely, as doing so would disrupt or halt production chains. Behind the scenes, there are still critical facilities such as hospitals, water supply pumping stations, and sewage treatment plants. Shutting them down would lead to a social and public utility collapse.

items.title: Triathlon Team Claims Historic European Championship Gold
items.summary: Three weeks after winning the silver medal at the World Championships in Hamburg, the Hungarian mixed triathlon relay team has written another chapter in sports history. With Márta Kropkó, Márk Dévay, Fanni Szalai, and Csongor Lehmann, the quartet was crowned European champions in the sprint distance on Saturday in Elbląg, Poland. In a dramatic race […] The post Triathlon Team Claims Historic European Championship Gold appeared first on Hungary Today.
items.body_text:
Swimmers from 60 countries took part in the iconic Hungarian open-water event after weather delays.Continue reading
Three weeks after winning the silver medal at the World Championships in Hamburg, the Hungarian mixed triathlon relay team has written another chapter in sports history. With Márta Kropkó, Márk Dévay, Fanni Szalai, and Csongor Lehmann, the quartet was crowned European champions in the sprint distance on Saturday in Elbląg, Poland. In a dramatic race made more challenging by a sudden change in weather, the Hungarians deservedly prevailed over the competition from Spain and Germany.
The competition demanded a grueling sprint program from each of the four team members: a 300-meter swim, an 8-kilometer bike ride, and a 1.6-kilometer run. A total of 20 nations competed, but the Hungarian team delivered by far the most consistent team performance over the entire race distance. In the end, anchor runner Csongor Lehmann crossed the finish line first, six seconds ahead of the second-place Spaniards and 20 seconds ahead of the third-place Germans.
Lead runner Márta Kropkó laid the foundation for the eventual victory.
She handed off the baton in second place, 11 seconds behind the leading Polish rival, but had already managed to build a small lead of one to two seconds over the rest of the chasing pack.
The second Hungarian athlete, Márk Dévay, had already cut the gap in half during the swim and caught up to the leaders on the first cycling leg. From there on, he and his Polish rival took turns leading the pack, increasing their lead over the main field to 20 seconds. Although Márk Dévay had to let the Pole pass him in the final meters after a thrilling sprint to the finish during the run, the tactic paid off.
Fanni Szalai took over in third place, three seconds behind the leader. She had already passed the Polish athlete during the swim, further extended her lead on the bike, and held onto that advantage through the run.
She handed off to anchor runner Csongor Lehmann with a 29-second lead over a strong group of five pursuers (Great Britain, France, Spain, Germany, and Poland).
Things got dramatic once again in the final kilometers. A heavy rain shower flooded the course and slowed the pace. While Csongor Lehmann crashed on the wet asphalt, the final cyclists from Great Britain, Spain, and Germany made up a lot of ground. The Hungarian athlete, however, showed nerves of steel. He jumped back on his bike and preserved a lead of seven to eight seconds heading into the final leg. There, only Spain’s Pelayo González Turrez was able to keep up with Csongor Lehmann, but the Hungarian accelerated once more in the final meters and sealed the historic gold medal.
After the triumph, Márta Kropkó offered insights into the emotional experience of a lead runner. “Being the first runner is actually a thankless job. Once you’re done, you have to spend another hour on the edge of your seat while your three teammates battle it out on the course. I screamed my heart out and hoped that no one would make a mistake. The only thing I did not have to worry about was everyone’s absolute determination. When Csongor fell, my heart skipped a beat for a moment, but he handled it brilliantly,” she explained. The Hungarian athlete also emphasized that
the World Championship silver medal in Hamburg gave the team the final boost of confidence that this lineup “has a lot of potential.”
Fanni Szalai also gave an all-around positive assessment. After a strong performance at the World Cup series in London the previous week, she arrived in top form. “We all came here feeling that gold was absolutely within reach. There was not a single decisive moment today—every single one of us gave it our all. This victory is the result of pure, perfect teamwork,” she emphasized.
With this European Championship title, the Hungarian delegation celebrates its third medal at the continental championships, after Zalán Hóbor won bronze medals in both the elite and U23 age group

items.title: Volt behajtási engedélye a betonkeverőnek, amely a belvárosban gázolt halálra egy biciklist
items.summary: A betonkeverő július 29-én gázolt el egy kerékpárost az Erzsébet körút és a Király utca kereszteződésében.
items.body_text:
Volt behajtási engedélye a betonkeverőnek, amely a belvárosban gázolt halálra egy biciklist
Érvényes behajtási engedéllyel rendelkezett az a betonkeverő, amely július 29-én halálra gázolt egy kerékpárost az Erzsébet körút és a Király utca kereszteződésében – írja a Hvg.hu a Budapest Közút tájékoztatása alapján.
A 23 éves nő éppen a körútról kanyarodott volna a Király utcába, amikor összeütközött a mellette haladó betonkeverővel. A teherautó alá szorult, és a helyszínen életét vesztette. Baranyi Krisztina később közölte, hogy az áldozat a ferencvárosi önkormányzat egyik köznevelési intézményében dolgozott. A BRFK közúti baleset gondatlan okozása miatt folytat eljárást, a sofőrt gyanúsítottként hallgatták ki.
A betonkeverő egész júliusra és a nap 24 órájára érvényes behajtási engedéllyel rendelkezett. Az engedély a belvároson belül nem jelölt ki kötelező útvonalat, ugyanakkor előírta, hogy a betonkeverő elsősorban főútvonalakon közlekedjen, és a korlátozott övezetet a lehető legrövidebb útvonalon érintse. A teherautót a Strabag egyik alvállakozója üzemeltette, a sofőr ennek a vállalkozásnak az alkalmazottja. A cég a Hvg kérdésére azt írta, minden súlyos balesetet belső vizsgálat keretében is részletesen kivizsgálnak. A baleset további körülményeiről a cég nem adott tájékoztatást, arra hivatkozva, hogy ezek az információk a hatósági eljárás részét képezik.
Korábban Karácsony Gergely főpolgármester közölte, hogy a BKK és a Budapest Közút felülvizsgálja a Nagykörút felújításának eddig elkészült terveit, és szükség esetén módosítja azokat, illetve egyéb intézkedések bevezetését is megfontolja. Hozzátette, hogy támogatják a KRESZ módosítását is, hogy a buszok és teherautók kanyarodási sebességét 10 km/h-ban korlátozzák.

items.title: „Nem tetszik ez nekem” – túl sok pénzt keres az Exxon Mobil és a Chevron Trump szerint
items.summary: Az amerikai elnök alacsonyabb benzinárakat követel az amerikai olajcégektől.
items.body_text:
„Nem tetszik ez nekem” – túl sok pénzt keres az Exxon Mobil és a Chevron Trump szerint
A magas benzinárak miatt Donald Trump hétfőn beleszállt az Exxon Mobil és Chevron amerikai olajcégekbe – az amerikai elnök szerint ugyanis túl sok pénzt keresnek, az iráni háború miatti ellátási gondokra hivatkozva.
„Nem tetszik ez nekem, és nekem kellene az utolsónak lenni, aki ezt mondja, mert én vagyok a szabad vállalkozás legnagyobb híve – senki sem nagyobb nálam” – mondta Trump a Politico szerint, majd konkrétan megnevezte az Egyesült Államok két nagy olajcégét, amelyek pár nappal ezelőtt kiugró negyedéves eredményeket jelentettek be, miközben az olajár, kisebb kilengésekkel ugyan, de még mindig magas szinten van az iráni háború miatt.
„Chevron, túl sok pénz. Exxon Mobil, túl sok, túl sok pénz” – mondta, hozzátéve, a profit egy részét a cégek vissza kellene, hogy adják az embereknek és csökkenteniük kell a fogyasztói árat. Trump azt is mondta, az olajárak úgyis „a mélypontra zuhannak”, amikor véget ér az Iránnal folytatott konfliktus – arról azonban, hogy valójában mikor folytatódnak a hétfőre belengetett tárgyalások, egyelőre nem lehet tudni.
Trumpnak egyébként kifejezetten fontos az iparág, ösztönzi a fúrásokat, és az amerikai energiatermelés bővítése központi eleme a programjának. Az amerikai elnök az utóbbi időben azonban többször is megpróbált nyomást gyakorolni a termelőkre, tartsák alacsony szinten az üzemanyagárakat – ennek pedig, a novemberi félidős választásokhoz közeledve egyre nagyobb a jelentősége. A benzin kiskereskedelmi ára több mint 30 százalékkal emelkedett azóta, hogy az Egyesült Államok és Izrael idén év elején megtámadta Iránt. Az olajcégektől elvárt profitkorlátozás azonban nincs összhangban azzal, hogy Trump mindeközben a hazai termelés maximalizálását is elvárja tőlük.
A Reuters azt írja, az amerikai elnök szavaira az amerikai olajcégeket képviselő szakmai szervezet, az American Petroleum Institute is reagált. „A mai magasabb árakat a globális kínálat, a kereslet, valamint a Hormuzi-szoros és más kritikus hajózási útvonalak körüli folyamatos bizonytalanság okozza – nem az egyes vállalatok.”

items.title: Nationwide inspection of battery industry-related plants announced in Hungary
items.summary: The previous, Fidesz government saw the battery industry as a potential pillar of Hungary’s economic growth. As a result, several battery plants were established in Hungary in recent years, despite locals' protests over environmental concerns.
items.body_text:
Nationwide inspection of battery industry-related plants announced in Hungary
A nationwide inspection program examining the entire operational chain of the battery industry in Hungary has been launched as of August 1, Minister of the Living Environment László Gajdos announced on Tuesday on his Facebook page.
Gajdos wrote that battery manufacturing can only operate in Hungary under stringent official oversight, transparent regulations and genuine accountability, thereby ensuring acceptance by society. The inspections will extend to the plants’ actual capacity, materials used, emissions, water consumption, and waste management, as well as to the facilities related to battery production, solvents, and the management of industrial waste, according to MTI.
According to the minister, the inspections will go beyond simply reviewing the submitted documents: the authorities will compare the data in the permits with the actual operations on-site and will inspect the entire process, covering everything from the route of the raw materials, through emissions, to waste management.
Where warranted, the authorities will collect samples and conduct laboratory tests; serious violations or hazards will result in immediate regulatory action.
According to Gajdos, the program’s goal is to identify and eliminate violations, as well as to tighten regulations, licensing practices, and official inspections. “I consider the health and safety of the Hungarian people and the protection of natural resources and the environment as my top priority,” the minister wrote in his post.
The Tisza government announced in early June that it was working on setting up an autonomous national environmental protection authority and that a nationwide inspection program would be launched at industrial facilities which pose the greatest environmental risk. It was also announced at that time that a nationwide plan for inspecting battery plants and other hazardous facilities would be finalized by the end of June, and that the regulation under which the locations of battery recycling plants could be designated by ministerial decision would be repealed. The goal is to ensure that, in the future, such investments are made based on uniform and transparent rules rather than on individual political decisions.
Along with the automotive industry, the previous, Fidesz-led government saw the battery industry as a potential pillar of Hungary’s economic growth. In line with this, over the past decade, it provided substantial government subsidies and offered an extraordinarily favourable regulatory and administrative environment for the sector. This attracted the world’s largest battery manufacturers to the country, and even the repeated protests of locals in the affected towns couldn’t prevent the construction of the multiple plants involved in battery production.
Zsolt Tárkányi, a representative of the Tisza Party in Parliament and the Parliamentary State Secretary of the Ministry of Transportation and Investment, previously said that a new authority—which will oversee the operations of battery factories and other key industrial facilities—could be established by September. According to the plans, in the event of serious violations, this authority will be authorised to impose fines amounting to billions of forints on the companies involved; furthermore, in extreme cases, it will be authorized to revoke all of their operating permits, which would effectively mean shutting them down.
The operation of a Chinese-owned battery plant in Debrecen was recently suspended due to serious environmental concerns. This spring, Telex reported on the previous government's cover-up of the serious occupational safety violations at the Samsung SDI factory in Göd. We previously also reported on the hidden hazards of waste handling in Hungary's battery boom.
For more quick, accurate, and impartial news from and about Hungary, subscribe to the Telex English newsletter!

Prague Kettlebell Brand Železná Koule Opens 600-Square-Metre Gym in Karlín
Prague Morning
Czech kettlebell training brand Železná Koule has opened its largest location yet at Danube House in Prague’s Karlín district.
The new 600-square-metre gym expands the brand’s presence in Prague and comes ahead of the next edition of its flagship Amazing 12 fitness programme.
Železná Koule has built a community around kettlebell training and coached workouts rather than the traditional self-service gym model. The company says more than 20,000 people have trained through its programmes since its launch.
At its Karlín location, members train under the guidance of coaches in small groups. The approach is designed to provide more personal instruction and a structured training environment, rather than simply giving members access to gym equipment.
The new location is also the latest venue for the company’s Amazing 12 programme, a 12-week fitness and body transformation course that combines regular training with nutrition guidance and ongoing support.
What is the Amazing 12 programme?
The programme is aimed at both people who are new to structured strength training and more experienced gym-goers looking for a more organised approach to their workouts.
Although the programme itself lasts 12 weeks, participants first complete a preparation week, making 13 weeks in total. During the programme, they take part in 64 training sessions, with one-hour workouts held every weekday under the supervision of a coach.
Groups are limited to a maximum of five participants, allowing coaches to work closely with each person throughout the programme.
The programme is designed to provide a structured routine covering exercise, nutrition and recovery, with progress tracked throughout the 12 weeks.
The next Amazing 12 programme starts on August 31, 2026, with places available at the new Karlín location as well as Železná Koule gyms in Smíchov and Strašnice.
The Karlín opening is part of the continued expansion of a Czech fitness brand that has developed a following around kettlebell-based training and small-group coaching. For people unfamiliar with the name, Železná Koule roughly translates from Czech as “iron ball,” referring to the kettlebell at the centre of its training approach.
More information about the Amazing 12 programme, including registration, is available at amazing12.cz.

items.body_text:
A New Bus Line to Prague Airport Could Launch This Autumn
Prague Morning
A new private bus service could soon connect Prague’s main railway station directly with Václav Havel Airport, offering passengers another option for getting between the city center and the airport.
Transport company Dinarica is planning to launch the service at the end of October. The route would run between the main railway station and the airport, providing a direct alternative to the Airport Express operated by České dráhy.
The company says it wants to address one of the main practical problems passengers face when travelling by bus to the airport — luggage storage.
Dinarica plans to use Setra and MAN buses equipped with air conditioning, seat belts and more spacious seating. Each vehicle will accommodate between 70 and 90 passengers.
The planned service would operate from morning until evening, with buses running approximately every two hours.
A one-way ticket is expected to cost around CZK 125, making the service considerably cheaper than the Airport Express. Its fare is set to rise to CZK 200 following the latest price increase.
Prague’s public transport system already offers cheaper ways to reach the airport. Trolleybus 59 and bus 100 connect Václav Havel Airport with the Prague public transport network, but neither provides a direct connection to the main railway station.
Both services are primarily designed as part of the regular city transport system.
If approved and launched as planned, the Dinarica service would give passengers another direct option between Prague’s main railway station and the airport, with a lower fare than the Airport Express.

items.body_text:
More Than Half of Czech Households Could Be Overpaying for Electricity
Prague Morning
A large number of Czech households may be paying more for electricity than necessary because they are using a distribution tariff that does not match their actual consumption.
A new analysis estimates that switching to a more suitable tariff could save households more than CZK 1.3 billion a year in total.
The analysis was conducted by energy company bezDodavatele.
The company examined electricity consumption at 1,132 household consumption points using the two most common household distribution tariffs, D01d and D02d.
According to data from the Energy Regulatory Office (ERÚ), D01d and D02d are used by around 65 percent of the approximately 6.5 million household consumption points in the Czech Republic.
The analysis found that changing the distribution tariff could reduce electricity costs for more than half of the households examined.
Many households never reconsider their tariff
One reason is that households often keep the same tariff for years without checking whether it still suits their electricity consumption.
A tariff that made sense when a household first connected to the electricity grid may no longer be the cheapest option after its consumption patterns have changed. Many consumers, however, do not regularly review the distribution tariff listed on their electricity bill.
According to the analysis, 53 percent of the households examined could have benefited from a different tariff. Their average potential saving was CZK 728 per year.
For some households, the difference was considerably larger, with potential savings reaching several thousand crowns annually.
Prague households show the highest potential
The analysis found differences between the country’s main electricity distribution areas.
In Prague, where electricity is distributed by PRE, changing the tariff could have been beneficial for 68 percent of the households included in the study. That was the highest proportion recorded among the three distribution zones.
In the EG.D distribution area, which covers much of southern Bohemia and Moravia as well as parts of the Vysočina, Zlín and Olomouc regions, the figure was 51.5 percent.
The lowest share was recorded in the ČEZ distribution area, where 46.3 percent of the households analyzed could potentially benefit from a different tariff.
The picture changes slightly when looking at the size of the potential savings. Although Prague had the highest proportion of households that could benefit from a tariff change, the largest average annual saving was recorded in the ČEZ Distribuce area, at CZK 833 per household.

The disruption, which temporarily removed the page from Meta, followed what the outlet and its journalists described as a “cyberattack,” amid a series of similar …
items.body_text:
Studio Monitori’s Facebook Page Temporarily Disabled Amid ‘Cyberattack’ Allegations
The Facebook page of Studio Monitori, a prominent Tbilisi-based investigative journalism outlet, was temporarily disabled on the morning of August 3, before being restored hours later at around 8 pm.
The disruption, which temporarily removed the page from Meta, followed what the outlet and its journalists described as a “cyberattack,” amid a series of similar attempts in recent months to take down Monitori’s investigative reports and its social media pages and channels, including on Facebook, YouTube and TikTok.
“An organized series of cyberattacks against Monitori has been underway for about a month,” Monitori journalist Mari Dudunia told online media outlet Publika on August 3. She said journalists had repeatedly received so-called phishing emails and that the outlet’s investigations and social media channels had been subjected to what appeared to be coordinated reporting campaigns aimed at having them suspended.
The Facebook page was disabled about a week after a similar case, in which Monitori’s YouTube channel that hosts years of its investigative work was temporarily removed from the platform. Dudunia said the YouTube incident followed reports submitted by “inauthentic accounts” run by so-called trolls. She added that the channel was later restored after Monitori complained to YouTube and the platform reviewed the case, finding no copyright violation.
Dudunia suggested that the reports against Monitori’s pages appeared to come from government-affiliated pages and accounts. Monitori has carried out a series of investigations into the wealth and activities of Georgian Dream figures and their affiliates, drawing continued criticism from government officials, while some of its findings were later supported by subsequent investigations.
Georgian Dream MP Nino Tsilosani appeared to welcome the temporary suspension on August 3. In a Facebook post sharing a card from pro-government broadcaster Imedi TV reporting that Monitori’s Facebook page had been “deleted,” she accused the outlet of spreading “lies and manipulations” over the years.
The latest suspension came just before Monitori was due to publish a follow-up video investigation into scam call centres. Ultimately published on August 4, the investigation builds on an international investigation published a year ago, in which Monitori was one of the participating media organizations that exposed how European and Canadian citizens were defrauded by scammers in Tbilisi-based call centres.
The latest investigation suggests that, although authorities froze the scammers’ property following the journalistic investigation, they have continued operating from another office in Tbilisi.

items.body_text:
Head of Georgian State Electrosystem, Country’s Major Grid Owner, Leaves Post After Two Nationwide Blackouts
The head of Georgian State Electrosystem (GSE), the country’s main electricity transmission grid owner, has left his post days after Georgia was hit by two nationwide blackouts on July 24-25.
Vano Zardiashvili, a former Georgian Dream MP who has headed GSE since 2025, was reported dismissed by Business Media Georgia (bm.ge) on August 2. The outlet cited anonymous sources that linked his alleged dismissal to preliminary findings by Georgia’s National Energy and Water Supply Regulatory Commission (GNERC), which acts as an independent regulator overseeing the electricity sector. A GSE representative, however, rejected that Zardiashvili was dismissed over GNERC’s findings, saying instead that he resigned himself.
The regulator’s preliminary findings came a week after the July 24 blackout, which GNERC said followed the disconnection of Georgia’s power system from Azerbaijan’s grid. The findings raised questions about the national grid’s protection systems and its ability to remain stable while operating in isolation.
According to Georgia’s Public Broadcaster, the GNERC working group said Georgia’s power system abruptly disconnected from Azerbaijan’s grid at around 00:10:49 on July 24. The system then had to operate on its own, causing frequency and voltage to fall. This triggered “cascading shutdowns” of power plants and consumers, eventually resulting in a “complete shutdown” of the power system.
The working group identified the 110 kV Geguti transmission line, owned by Energo-Pro Georgia, the largest private electricity distribution and generation company supplying power to customers outside Tbilisi, as one factor in the incident.
It said that the GSE “should not have waited” for new fast-acting protection systems to be installed, but should instead have adjusted the protection and automation systems already in place. According to the regulator, this could have reduced the risk of Georgia being disconnected from Azerbaijan and helped keep the power system stable.
The working group said the issue requires further investigation in two areas: why the connection with Azerbaijan was cut, and why Georgia’s power system could not remain stable while operating on its own.
Separately, the State Security Service of Georgia (SSSG) is investigating the July 24-25 blackouts under “sabotage.”. The outages also affected the occupied Abkhazia region.
Georgian Dream Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze told journalists on August 3 that he “cannot say” whether Zardiashvili was dismissed, adding that “the decision in this regard is made directly by the Economy Ministry.” He added that “many [good] things were done in the power system under Vano Zardiashvili’s leadership.”

items.body_text:
DW Launches EU-Funded Georgian-Language News Service
Deutsche Welle, Germany’s international public broadcaster, launched an EU-funded Georgian-language news service on Instagram on August 3, with plans to expand to additional platforms at a later stage.
The new service will cover stories from Georgia, Europe and around the world, offering what its launch announcement described as “reliable, objective, and timely” information on current affairs.
The project is funded by the European Union and is part of the “European Information Shield Initiative,” a joint project led by DW and Fact-Checking and Media Literacy (FMM), together with Polish international broadcaster TVP World. The initiative aims to “strengthen independent journalism and counter disinformation” in the South Caucasus, DW said in a July 21 press release.
The Georgian-language service is part of a wider regional effort as FMM has established an Armenian-language offering, while TVP World has launched an Azerbaijani-language service, according to the same press release. The three projects are expected to cooperate and share content, with the aim of expanding the reach of independent journalism across the region.
The initiative is funded for an initial 18 months and builds on previous European cooperation projects involving DW and FMM, including ENTR and InfoMigrants.
German daily Taz reported that the Georgian editorial team will consist of five to seven journalists, most of whom are based in Germany. One journalist is expected to join from Georgia. The newspaper identified Zura Karaulashvili as head of the Georgian-language editorial team.
In late April, Polish public broadcaster TVP launched VT Sakartvelo, a Georgian-language news service broadcast.

items.title: Ingush women urge regional authorities to save medieval tower complex from collapse
items.summary: The women say the foundation of the Two Rivals’ Towers is eroding.
items.body_text:
A group of Ingush women have recorded a video appeal urging the authorities to take urgent measures to preserve the medieval Two Rivals’ Towers complex in the Dzheyrakh district. According to the women, the architectural monument is at risk of collapse because the rock on which it stands is deteriorating.
The video was published on social media on Saturday and addressed to the republic’s Head Makhmud-Ali Kalimatov, Parliamentary Speaker Magomet Tumgoev, and MPs Muslim Tatriev and Bekhan Barakhoev.
In the appeal, the 10 women say they have been monitoring the condition of the complex for a long time and believe the situation has become critical. They also call on the EU-sanctioned billionaire and founder of the SAFMAR charitable foundation, Mikhail Gutseriev, to take personal charge of efforts to preserve the site. Gutseriev has financed the restoration of Ingushetia’s medieval tower complexes for several years.
‘The damage appeared only a few years ago and has been increasing rapidly. The site is located in a hard-to-reach area, and without specialised equipment, machinery, and the necessary funding, we are unfortunately unable to save it ourselves’, the appeal says.
The authors stress that the issue concerns not only an architectural monument but also an important part of the republic’s historical heritage.
The Ingush authorities had not publicly responded to the appeal at the time of publication.
The Two Women’s Towers, also known as the Two Rivals’ Towers, are located in mountainous Ingushetia in the Dzheyrakh district. The complex is regarded as one of the best-known examples of medieval Ingush architecture and is associated with a local legend about two rival women, two wives of the same man, from which it takes its modern name. It forms part of the Dzheyrakh-Assa State Historical, Architectural, and Natural Museum-Reserve.
The preservation of Ingushetia’s medieval tower complexes has long been the subject of public debate. The main threats to many of these structures are natural geological processes, including soil erosion, rockfalls, and seismic activity. In addition, some monuments spent decades without conservation work or systematic maintenance.
In recent years, the Ingush authorities have implemented an extensive programme to restore medieval towers across the republic. Traditional construction materials and techniques have been used to reinforce endangered structures, while restoration work has been carried out under the supervision of cultural heritage specialists.
However, the restoration programme has repeatedly drawn criticism. Heritage experts and conservation specialists have argued that some projects employed modern materials and construction methods which, in their view, undermine the historical authenticity of the monuments. The regional authorities, meanwhile, have maintained that the work complies with approved conservation plans and is necessary to prevent the irreversible destruction of the sites.
Mountainous Ingushetia is home to one of the largest concentrations of medieval tower architecture in the North Caucasus. The region contains hundreds of residential, defensive, and semi-defensive towers, as well as churches, mausoleums, and other monuments, most dating from the 14th to the 18th centuries. Many of the towers have federal cultural heritage status and are among Ingushetia’s main tourist attractions.

items.title: Facebook page of Georgian investigative outlet Studio Monitor removed
items.summary: Georgian investigative outlet Studio Monitor’s Facebook page was removed on Monday.
items.body_text:
The Facebook page of Georgian investigative outlet Studio Monitor was removed on Monday, just over a week after the outlet’s YouTube channel was taken down and later restored following an appeal.
The removal comes amid growing concerns over media freedom in Georgia, where independent and critical media outlets have increasingly reported legal pressure and restrictions on their work.
A screenshot shared by Studio Monitor journalist Marika Dudunia shows that Meta, Facebook’s parent company, cited copyright infringement as the reason for removing the page. Studio Monitor has rejected the claim.
Speaking to OC Media, Dudunia said the outlet hoped Facebook would restore the page, as YouTube had after reviewing its appeal.
‘The same thing happened a week ago with YouTube. We complained, and YouTube accepted our complaint, learned that these were not authentic complaints and were intentionally made reports, and then they reinstated [our channel]’, Dudunia said.
Dudunia added that the outlet did not know what prompted Facebook’s action. She noted that Studio Monitor had announced a new investigation into alleged call centre scams three days earlier, which was due to be published on Monday.
‘We think that this is a well-organised attack against us. They want to silence us and they want no one to see our journalistic investigations’, Dudunia said.
She added that the outlet had repeatedly faced digital threats following the publication of high-profile investigations, including phishing attempts and coordinated reporting campaigns targeting its content on social media platforms.
On 1 July, after publishing an investigation into alleged links between Georgian construction companies and a network of unlicensed online casinos, Studio Monitor said a group of users had begun reporting all related content on YouTube and Facebook. At the time, the outlet said that ‘as a result of a coordinated cyber-attack, Meta informed us that several Monitor materials were deleted from their platform’.
The latest investigation announced by Studio Monitor concerns an alleged international call centre fraud scheme.
The Georgian Charter of Journalistic Ethics has condemned the removal of Studio Monitor’s Facebook page, describing it as a cyber-attack and expressing solidarity with the outlet.
In a statement published on Monday, the Charter said this was the third time in two months that Studio Monitor had faced disruption linked to alleged cyber-attacks. It called on Meta to investigate the incident and restore the deleted page.
‘Cyber-criminals operate with impunity in the country, and large resources are spent on troll-bot factories, which regularly attack organisations, experts and activists, media outlets, and journalists critical of the Georgian Dream’, their statement read.
Founded in 2005, Studio Monitor is one of Georgia’s most prominent investigative journalism organisations and has produced hundreds of investigations and in-depth reports.
Update, 4 August: Studio Monitor announced later on Monday that its Facebook page had been restored after being unavailable for several hours. The outlet said the page had been blocked ‘as a result of a cyberattack’. It thanked supporters for their backing and said it would continue its work, urging readers to ‘wait for our new investigation into fraudulent call centres’.

items.title: Number of fathers taking parental leave doubles in five years
items.summary: Despite the increase, women still take more parental leave than men, and in longer stretches.
items.body_text:
Summer is now the busiest time of year for fathers taking parental leave in Finland, according to benefits agency Kela.
For at least the past five years, the number of men receiving parental leave benefits generally peaks in July and August.
Last August, just over 18,000 fathers received parental leave payments, accounting for a third of all recipients. By comparison, men made up just 26 percent of recipients in March, when fewer than 13,000 fathers were on leave.
Mothers' use of parental leave, however, remains relatively steady throughout the year. Women still take longer and more frequent periods of parental leave than men.
Why summer?
According to Kela’s research manager Anneli Miettinen, many families choose summer so they can spend time together before their child starts early childhood education.
"Many parents want their child to begin daycare in August or September. Fathers may use parental leave after the mother so the child can start daycare later in the autumn," Miettinen said.
Another reason is timing. July and August have consistently been among Finland's busiest birth months, and many fathers take leave immediately after their child is born.
Associate Professor of Sociology Satu Helske from the University of Turku said some fathers may also schedule leave at times that best suit their employer, although it is unclear whether this specifically explains the summer peak.
Responses to a recent Yle questionnaire also suggested that many fathers deliberately overlap parental leave with family holidays so they can spend more time together.
Fathers' parental leave has increased
Fathers' use of parental leave has increased significantly in recent years.
According to Kela, men accounted for just under 23 percent of all paid parental leave days in 2025, compared to just over 10 percent five years earlier.
The increase has been driven largely by Finland's family leave reform, introduced in August 2022, which aimed to encourage fathers to take more leave and offered families greater flexibility in how to share the leave periods.
Research also shows fathers are increasingly taking leave independently rather than only alongside the other parent.
According to Helske, fathers are most likely to take parental leave when they are first-time parents.
Helske said that ongoing research also suggests that workplace culture plays an important role.
"If one father has taken a longer parental leave, it can encourage other fathers to do the same," she said.
