items.title: The Man Who Was Kidnapped Twice
items.summary: Thousands of people in Nigeria have been held for ransom by bandit groups. One professor escaped his captors—only to be abducted again.
items.body_text:
Izuchukwu Anyanwu, a university lecturer in Abuja, Nigeria, came home one evening and settled in for a quiet night. It was September, 2023, and he had spent the afternoon playing soccer with friends on the campus of Veritas University, where he taught. He was tired and was running a fever, so he took a shower and had some tea and bread; he also took medicine for malaria, in case he had contracted it. His wife, Immaculata, put their infant daughter to sleep, then went to bed herself. Around midnight, Anyanwu was watching a political-news program on TV when he heard a noise at the outer door of the veranda. It sounded as though someone was trying to break in. There had been a power outage that night, and he was using a solar-energy system to run the TV. He opened a window but couldn’t see who was there. “I was scared,” he told me recently. “I started shouting, ‘Who is that? Who is that?’ ”
At thirty-eight, Anyanwu is slim and bearded, with a youthful face. He grew up in a small town in the southeast of the country, then went to Veritas, a Catholic university, to get a master’s in political theory. He eventually was offered a teaching job, and rented a place in Zuma II, a neighborhood just outside the university’s gates where many faculty members live. It’s on the northern outskirts of the city in the rocky foothills of some nearby mountains. “I felt safe,” he said. “My hope was to build up my academic profile and eventually have my own house here.” His daughter would be turning one in February, and the family was planning a big celebration.
As the noises grew louder, Anyanwu tried calling a neighborhood-watch group, then some friends, but the calls didn’t connect. His wife woke up, and the two of them screamed out the window for help. Then the intruders broke the locks. “That is when I saw that it was over,” he said. Seventeen men entered his house, some wearing camouflage and carrying AK-47s, rocket-propelled-grenade launchers, and machine guns. “They were armed like people going to war,” he recalled. They made Anyanwu and Sunday Ujah, a twenty-year-old man who lived with the family and helped with housework, lie on the floor in the sitting room, then demanded that Immaculata show them where the valuables were kept. Anyanwu protested, telling them that he was not a politician and had no money. Since there was little of value, the men took rice, groundnuts, soft drinks, and powdered milk. A few finished Anyanwu’s leftover tea and bread.
The men took away Anyanwu’s and Ujah’s phones, and brought the two to a neighboring house to kidnap a local trader. Then they all set off on foot toward the mountains. The captives carried the stolen food. Anyanwu was still in his house clothes: shorts, a polo shirt, and slippers. They walked through the forest for hours. The area was wild and uninhabited, but the bandits moved through it with practiced ease. “There were those that went ahead of us and then gave signals for us to continue,” Anyanwu said. The kidnappers were all Fulani, a Muslim-majority ethnic group whose members live largely in the north of the country. Considering their sophisticated weaponry, he wondered if they were associated with the Islamist militant group Boko Haram, but the men didn’t give a name for their group or profess any particular ideology.
They set up camp in a forest near a village called Tunga Maje. Anyanwu knew their location because he saw the address of a local manufacturer on a package of bread that the kidnappers bought. He and the other two hostages were kept in a cave. It was the rainy season, and he had to put leaves on the wet ground to sleep. He could hear the voices of another group of hostages somewhere in the forest, out of sight. “They kept them apart from us,” he said.

Home affairs ministers are meeting this morning as the fallout of the Ceuta crisis continues to roil Europe.
Last week’s sudden influx of migrants into the Spanish exclave — most of whom have since returned — sparked heated exchanges between European leaders. On the show, hosts Zoya Sheftalovich and Ian Wishart preview whether today’s emergency meeting can cool tensions, and what measures the Commission may propose to address concerns across the bloc.
Next, a drought in Hungary and Romania could grind nuclear power plants to a halt since the River Danube has fallen too low to cool their reactors. Budapest and Bucharest are on high alert over the risk of an energy crisis in the coming days.
Plus: The Belgium push to encourage young people to sign up for voluntary military service appears to have worked, as the program starting Sept. 1 is already fully booked.

items.title: Even if Hamas disarms, the challenge in Gaza will be accountability
items.summary: History suggests that without legal and moral accountability, reconciliation and durable peace will remain elusive.
items.body_text:
The reported agreement by Hamas to a “complete disarmament” has renewed speculation about what a future beyond war might look like for Gaza. It has also left many unanswered questions.
Under the roadmap negotiated through US President Donald Trump’s Board of Peace, Hamas and other Palestinian armed groups would surrender their weapons in stages.
Israel would withdraw its forces from Gaza, and governance would gradually transfer to a Palestinian transitional administration supported by international monitors and an “international stabilisation force”.
But while Hamas has reportedly accepted the roadmap, implementation remains conditional on Israeli withdrawal. For its part, Israel has expressed “serious security concerns” about Hamas’ true intentions and said it will not withdraw until Hamas disarms.
For now, Gaza remains engulfed in conflict. Military operations continue, civilians are suffering, and the political obstacles to any agreement remain considerable.
But the prospect of disarmament raises a broader question: if the guns eventually fall silent, what happens to the allegations of war crimes under international law, and how can peace be built between communities carrying profound trauma?
International law in limbo
History suggests accountability will have to be central to any lasting agreement. In the former Yugoslavia, Rwanda and Northern Ireland, this has been a long, difficult process.
Israelis continue to live with the effects of 2023’s October 7 attacks. Gazans, meanwhile, have endured immense civilian suffering, large-scale destruction, displacement and loss of life.
Claims of war crimes and crimes against humanity have been directed at Hamas leaders and Israeli political and military officials.
The Gaza Peace Plan unveiled last year – the basis of this latest agreement – is particularly contentious because it appears to grant complete amnesty to Hamas leaders, precluding the possibility of accountability for alleged crimes under international law.
Surprisingly, there is no mention of amnesty for members of the Israeli Defence Forces or senior Israeli political leaders.
More broadly, the settlement is focused primarily on governance and security. But if questions of justice and accountability are sidelined, profound grievances will be left unresolved – which may ultimately undermine the prospects for lasting peace and meaningful reconciliation.
Read more: Trump is hailing it as a ‘breakthrough’, but will Hamas actually disarm in Gaza?
For many on both sides, the question is not simply how the conflict ends, but whether their suffering and trauma are acknowledged and justice is done. This also brings the role of the International Criminal Court (ICC) back into focus.
Its investigation into alleged crimes committed in Gaza, the West Bank and East Jerusalem began in 2014. In 2024, the court issued arrest warrants for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, former Defence Minister Yoav Gallant and Hamas military commander Mohammed Deif.
The ICC found reasonable grounds to believe that crimes within its jurisdiction may have been committed. That investigation continues, despite Israel’s objections to the court’s jurisdiction.
The latest developments are happening at the most fraught moment in the ICC’s history. items.title: Do we really need 10,000 steps a day?
items.summary: The infamous 10,000 steps per day recommendation didn’t come from a research laboratory.
items.body_text:
You’ve probably heard that hitting 10,000 steps a day is the key to health and longevity.
This magic number feels like a medical rule, handed down by doctors across the globe.
But where did it come from? And is it even true?
Let’s step back to Japan in 1964
Believe it or not, but the infamous 10,000 steps a day recommendation didn’t come from a research laboratory.
In fact, it is not scientific at all.
It came from a Japanese pedometer called the manpo-kei which translates to “10,000-step meter”.
This pedometer went on sale just after the 1964 Tokyo Olympics, at a time when there was a growing worry people in Japan weren’t moving enough.
The number was mainly chosen was because it was catchy and easy to remember. The Japanese kanji character for 10,000 – 万 – even looks a little like a walking person, which may have played a role in deciding on the number.
So 10,000 was a slogan to sell a step-counter, not an evidence-based recommendation.
So many ideas about what makes us sick, or keeps us well, sound plausible. Early studies might sound promising. But then something gets twisted. In this series, we investigate how a grain of truth ends up as a common health myth. And we untangle what went wrong along the way.
So what does the research say?
Getting 10,000 steps a day can be a useful goal, and it will have a positive impact on your health. But you can reap health benefits from even less.
A recently published systematic review combined the results of 57 studies and more than 160,000 adults to examine the relationship between daily steps and health. Interestingly, they found 7,000 steps a day was where health benefits were maximised.
Reaching 7,000 steps a day was linked to a 47% lower risk of dying early, a 25% lower risk of cardiovascular disease (heart disease and stroke), a 14% lower risk of type 2 diabetes, a 38% lower risk of dementia, a 22% lower some of depression and a 28% lower risk of falls.
Some health benefits started well before 7,000 steps.
The researchers found going from about 2,000 to 4,000 steps a day makes a real difference. These health benefits then increase again slightly from 4,000 to 7,000 steps a day, after which the benefits start to plateau.
These results align closely with other research looking at all types of physical activity, where going from being inactive to moderately active yields the largest health improvements. Moving from a moderate to high level of activity does provide additional benefits, but these are much smaller in magnitude.
Why walking is good for you
Walking is a form of “aerobic” exercise. It raises your heart rate and places stress on your respiratory, muscular and cardiovascular systems.
If you do it regularly, it can improve your heart and metabolic health, and reduce your bodyweight.
Walking can also reduce stress and improve mental health, possibly due improvements in feelings of self-esteem and self-efficacy that comes with regular movement.
Steps versus minutes
There is some additional nuance that needs to be considered when discussing how far you walk each day: how hard you walk.
Most people choose a walking pace that pushes them into the realm of “moderate intensity” exercise. However, the health benefits of exercise scale up with exercise intensity: you get more bang for your buck from more intense exercise.
So, if you pick up the pace and move towards a vigorous exercise intensity (where it’s hard to maintain a conversation), you will get larger health benefits in less time. This is why official exercise guidelines treat 75 minutes of vigorous activity as roughly equal to 150 minutes of moderate activity.
With this in mind, rather than focusing on steps, you might be better off focusing on the number of minutes you accumulate each week.
Recent research even suggests short bursts of high-intensity exercise spread across the day can have surprising health benefits.
So, if you’re short on time, walking faster is one of the simplest ways to get more out of that same walk.

items.title: Kyrgyzstan’s Dordoi Bazaar: a world made from shipping containers and a city within a city
items.summary: Every container opens onto its own distinct social world.
items.body_text:
When I left Ainura’s container-shop at the Dordoi Bazaar in Bishkek, the capital of Kyrgyzstan, I found the market eerily quiet. I had not noticed the passing of time, while she generously shared her life story with me.
Walking towards the mini-bus stop at the square in front of the bazaar, the echo of her words mixed with the end-of-day soundscape at Dordoi: the heavy slam of container-shops’ metal doors and the resonant clang of heavy padlocks clicking into place.
The Insights section is committed to high-quality longform journalism. Our editors work with academics from many different backgrounds who are tackling a wide range of societal and scientific challenges.
A moment later, only the sound of stray plastic wrappings stirred up by the last vendors and customers heading home, hinted at the day’s bustling activity.
Soon, the cleaners would sweep them down the pathways between the containers and children would try to snatch the recyclables. Answering my question about why she thinks Dordoi is a good place to work, Ainura explained:
Here in Kyrgyzstan, we can’t rely on the state. Dordoi feeds the country. It feeds our families; and it allowed me to start a new life after I had left my husband.
Ainura is one of thousands of people – many of them women – who found a new livelihood at Dordoi after life took an unexpected turn. Estimates of people working there range from 30,000 to 150,000, depending on whether auxiliary jobs, such as food hawkers, drivers, packers and carriers are included.
In 2025, these diverse economic activities generated roughly US$7.9 million in tax revenue: a substantial contribution to the city’s public finances.
Spanning more than 100 hectares and built from up to 60,000 double and triple-stacked shipping containers, Dordoi stands as one of Kyrgyzstan’s most important economic engines since the country gained independence in 1991.
More than a trading centre, Dordoi is a city within a city. Beyond shops and storage spaces, it also has currency exchanges, medical centres, a fire station, hotels, a gym, beauty salons and a mosque.
Its liveliness is equally reflected in the languages spoken along its aisles. While Russian and Kyrgyz remain the languages of commerce, Dungan, Uyghur, Uzbek, Tajik, and Chinese can also be heard, revealing the extensive trading networks that converge here from across Central Asia and beyond. Traders sell almost anything that can be bought, packed and shipped – from sewing needles and refrigerators to cars and spare parts.
Yet clothing remains Dordoi’s lifeblood. Textiles, knitwear and ready-made garments dominate the trade, arriving chiefly from China and Turkey alongside an increasing volume of locally produced apparel.
At the heart of the market, the central passageway serves as both a shopping boulevard and the bazaar’s main artery. Cart pushers weave through the crowded aisles, shouting “Jol, jol, jol, jooool, daroga!” (“Make way!” both in Kyrgyz and Russian) as they manoeuvre heavily laden carts through the throngs of daily visitors.
Threading their way through the crowds, they deliver goods to packing stations near the long-distance bus terminal, where workers compress merchandise into tightly packed bales and sacks. Every centimetre matters in the effort to minimise shipping costs.
By midday, the pace begins to slow. The air fills with the scent of roasting meat and fresh dough as food stalls offer a culinary map of Central Asia, from Dungan laghman and Uzbek plov to Uyghur samsa.
Tea vendors, coffee sellers and fruit merchants weave through the crowds, while – to my own delight – a growing number of barista coffee shops have become an increasingly visible part of the market landscape.

items.body_text:
Israel is not 'testing' its ceasefires. It's violating them
How many people do you need to kill before you’ve violated a ceasefire?
One, surely. But what about two? 10? 100?
Or how about more than 1,200? That’s how many Palestinians Israel has killed in Gaza since agreeing to an ostensible ceasefire with Hamas in October.
Israel has also continued to pummel southern Lebanon, despite a “ceasefire” there. But the western media appears to see no violations at all. Instead, it sees ceasefires that are “fragile”, “tested”, “strained” or “shaky”.
Given that news reporting is supposed to rely on precision and accuracy, you’d imagine organisations such as the BBC, Reuters, the Associated Press and CNN have read the terms of the deal that was signed between Israel and Hamas in Egypt. It’s unequivocal, and there really isn’t much room for interpretation.

Once the prerequisites were met, which they were, the text said that “all military operations, including aerial and artillery bombardment and targeting operations will be suspended”.
Snuffed out
It’s worth pausing on those words: “all military operations, including aerial and artillery bombardment and targeting operations will be suspended”.
Now square that with more than 1,000 dead Palestinians. Square it with the fact that many were women and children. Square it with the Israeli attack on southern Lebanon that killed school principal Esperanza Ghandour, her mother, a domestic worker and a Syrian labourer as they travelled together in a car.
Square it with the eight people killed at a Palestinian funeral last month. And dare try to square it with the Israeli attack on Gaza that killed Firas al-Masri; his wife, Salsabeel; and their three daughters and son.
None of these firmly established truths seem to stop international journalists from abandoning their duty to call things what they are
They were snuffed out by an occupying force as they slept in their family home, a place that is supposed to be one of love, safety and security.
I could not find a single report in the western media that described the massacre of the Masri household as a ceasefire violation. That’s a pattern across similar atrocities.
Israel said it was targeting a Hamas member without, as usual, providing evidence. But let’s assume for illustrative purposes that Firas al-Masri was in Hamas. After all, since the bogus October agreement, whenever Israel claims it has killed a Hamas member, the western media seems fine with it.
But who did Israel agree the ceasefire with? Yes, Hamas.
None of these firmly established truths seem to stop international journalists from abandoning their duty to call things what they are.
Double standards
A Reuters report on the targeted killing of the Masri family captured some of the horror, and quoted Masri’s father as he mourned the loss of his son, his daughter-in-law, his grandson and three granddaughters.
But despite that, the news agency managed to write 500 words - which also catalogued five other Israeli attacks on Gaza in the preceding days - without coming even close to saying that Israel had violated the ceasefire.
Instead, Reuters treated the truce as an existing reality, not a fiction that is ignored on a daily basis, using this remarkable sentence construction: “The latest deaths add to a toll of more than 1,160 Palestinians, mostly civilians, killed by Israeli attacks since an October ceasefire between Israel and Hamas militants took effect.”

items.title: Families await word of loved ones after deadly Morocco-Spain crossing
items.summary: Families in Morocco are desperately searching for missing relatives days after a deadly mass crossing into Spain's enclave of Ceuta, while thousands of migrants who remain in the territory queue for their first food aid after days without assistance.
items.body_text:
Morocco
Families in Morocco are desperately searching for missing relatives days after a deadly mass crossing into Spain's enclave of Ceuta, while thousands of migrants who remain in the territory queue for their first food aid after days without assistance.
Anxious families gathered near the border in Fnideq on Monday, hoping for news of loved ones who crossed into Ceuta during last week's unprecedented migrant surge.
Many said they had lost contact with sons and relatives after they entered the Spanish enclave.
Some had received a brief phone call confirming their arrival before communication suddenly stopped.
Spanish authorities say at least 72 migrants died during the crossing, with many drowning at sea and others killed in a stampede.
Several people remain unaccounted for, leaving families uncertain whether they are alive or dead.
The majority of migrants returned voluntarily by Friday, but groups of young men were still making their way back across the border on Monday.
Food aid reaches stranded migrants
In Ceuta, dozens of migrants queued under police supervision on Monday to receive what journalists on the ground understood to be the first food distribution in four days.
Many of those waiting were among the thousands who crossed from Morocco during the migration crisis that began on Thursday.
Authorities handed out food and water as migrants lined up in orderly queues.
Spanish officials estimate that between 3,000 and 5,000 of the roughly 60,000 people who entered Ceuta have avoided expulsion, including about 860 unaccompanied minors.
International concern grows
The mass crossing has intensified the debate over migration in Europe. Italy temporarily suspended the Schengen open-border agreement with Spain, while France announced tighter border controls.
The United States also voiced support for Spain, blaming the crisis on policies it said encouraged illegal migration into Europe.
Meanwhile, some migrants who returned to Morocco described a border that was effectively left open, saying security forces did little to stop thousands from crossing into the Spanish enclave.

items.title: Ugandan Opposition Leader Kizza Besigye in intensive care, wife says
items.summary: Ugandan opposition leader Kizza Besigye is reportedly in intensive care after his condition dramatically worsened in custody. His wife says the 70-year-old is now in critical condition at Mulago Hospital in Kampala, with medical sources describing him as unresponsive.
items.body_text:
Uganda
Ugandan opposition leader Kizza Besigye is in intensive care in hospital, his wife and medical sources said on Thursday, as the UN blasted a wider crackdown on dissent. Besigye, 70, has been in custody and facing treason charges over an alleged plot against veteran President Yoweri Museveni, who has been in power since 1986.
At a court appearance on Wednesday, Besigye rejected state-appointed lawyers. He was expressing anger at his own representatives being refused when he collapsed. His wife Winnie Byanyima, the executive director of UNAIDS, wrote on X: "He has been admitted to the ICU at Mulago Hospital (in Kampala).
"He is unconscious, unable to speak, and unresponsive even to a pain stimulus." A spokeswoman for the hospital, Gladys Baligonzaki Kajura, confirmed to AFP that Besigye had been admitted. "He is at the intensive care unit. He was admitted last evening and his condition is being managed," she added, without elaborating.
A medical source said, under condition of anonymity, that Besigye was taken to hospital on Wednesday evening and said he was in a "critical condition and unresponsive". Besigye, a former personal physician to Museveni, has been in the government's crosshairs since he joined the opposition more than 25 years ago.
He was abducted in neighbouring Kenya in 2024 and reappeared in Uganda, where he was brought before a military tribunal until the case was transferred to a civilian court. Before he collapsed, one of his defence lawyers -- the former mayor of Kampala Erias Lukwago -- was arrested while the other, former justice minister Martha Karua, was banned from entering the country.
Uganda has imposed a widening crackdown on opposition figures, lawyers and independent media in recent months. On Thursday, the Ugandan courts again refused to release Lukwago on bail. He was abducted from his home by the army then charged with failing to report treason. In early July, Lukwago likened his continued detention to "a death sentence" as he had chronic health problems affecting notably his lungs and spine. The judge at the latest bail hearing justified a refusal to free him because Lukwago did not have a certificate from his doctor stating that he cannot be treated in prison.
Besigye has been hospitalised three times since he was taken into custody. He was admitted briefly in February 2025 after a hunger strike and again earlier this year. His wife has repeatedly criticised his detention conditions, describing them as inhumane and alleging a plot to kill him. In Geneva, UN rights chief Volker Turk said the crackdown on dissent was twinned with a gradual erosion of the rule of law, increased military involvement in civilian institutions, and shrinking civic space.
"I am appalled that the authorities are increasingly targeting any form of dissent, and deepening restrictions on the fundamental freedoms of all those living in Uganda," he said in a statement. "Those who dare to speak out are silenced." Since Museveni, 81, was re-elected for a seventh term in January, repression has increased against all those perceived to oppose the government, the statement from Turk's office said.
According to their information, at least 50 opposition leaders and supporters, five human rights defenders and five journalists have been subjected to human rights violations since then, including enforced disappearance, torture and ill-treatment.
Ten leading civil society organisations have been suspended since January, while others have been closely scrutinised and, at times, subjected to harassment, it added. The UN rights office said it had also received information about increased military involvement in civilian institutions, while some media outlets have been forced to close temporarily.

The bodies of Zimbabwean national Nothabo Zandile Tshuma and her two daughters have arrived in Harare ahead of their burial in Bulawayo. The trio were allegedly killed in the United Kingdom last month, while the children's father remains in custody in South Africa.
The bodies of Nothabo Zandile Tshuma and her two daughters landed at Robert Gabriel Mugabe International Airport in Harare on Monday morning before being transferred to the family's home in Gwabalanda, Bulawayo.
Relatives and mourners gathered to pay their final respects ahead of the funeral on Tuesday.
Murder investigation continues
The three are alleged to have been killed on July 3 in the United Kingdom. Investigators suspect Nothabo's husband, Ndodana Mkhanyisi Tshuma, who is also the father of the two girls, was responsible for their deaths.
Suspect held in South Africa
Ndodana Mkhanyisi Tshuma remains in police custody in South Africa after allegedly fleeing there following the incident.
Authorities in the United Kingdom and South Africa are continuing legal proceedings related to the case, including efforts linked to the ongoing criminal investigation.

items.title: What Liberia can teach a world in search of peace
items.summary: At a time when many question whether sustainable peace is still achievable, Liberia offers a quiet but powerful reminder that even the deepest wounds of conflict can heal.
items.body_text:
Recently, I had the opportunity of addressing community peacebuilders in Myanmar, reflecting on Liberia’s long journey from conflict to peace. And while every country’s history is unique, the search for lasting peace raises remarkably similar questions. How do societies rebuild trust after violence? How do former adversaries learn to coexist? And what transforms a fragile peace into a lasting one?
These questions are particularly relevant today. The world is witnessing a troubling resurgence of armed conflict, political polarisation, and humanitarian crises. From Africa to Europe, the Middle East, and Asia, millions of people continue to live with the devastating consequences of war.
Liberian resilience
Liberia endured two devastating civil wars between 1989 and 2003. Hundreds of thousands of people lost their lives. Families were displaced, communities were torn apart, public institutions collapsed, and trust — the very foundation of peaceful societies — was deeply fractured.
Yet amid the tragedy, Liberia also demonstrated something remarkable: the extraordinary resilience of ordinary people determined to rebuild their country and reclaim their future. These experiences deepened my conviction that while the international community can help create the conditions for peace, sustainable peace cannot be imported. It must be built patiently by the people who will ultimately live with it.
Following the end of conflict, Liberia benefited enormously from international solidarity. The United Nations peacekeeping mission helped restore the security necessary for political dialogue, the return of refugees, democratic elections, and institutional recovery. International partners supported governance reforms, infrastructure reconstruction and economic revival.
These contributions were indispensable. But they were never sufficient on their own. The real work of peacebuilding began after the guns fell silent.
Rebuilding trust among citizens
Peace proved to be far more than the absence of violence. It required rebuilding trust among neighbours who had once feared one another. It demanded restoring confidence in public institutions, strengthening the rule of law, expanding educational opportunities, promoting accountable governance, and creating hope for future generations.
Perhaps the most enduring lesson from Liberia is that local ownership determines whether peace will last.
International organisations can facilitate dialogue, provide technical expertise, mobilise resources, and accompany countries through difficult transitions. They cannot, however, replace the determination of citizens to reconcile with one another and build a shared future.
In Liberia, traditional leaders, religious communities, civil society organisations, women, youth, and local authorities all played indispensable roles in healing divisions and rebuilding relationships. Much of this work occurred quietly, far from international headlines. Yet it formed the foundation upon which lasting peace and stability was gradually rebuilt.
Another lesson is the importance of inclusion. Women were not simply victims of Liberia’s conflict; they became some of its most influential peacebuilders. Their leadership helped unite communities across political, ethnic, and religious divides and demonstrated that sustainable peace depends upon the meaningful participation of all members of society.
Young people likewise represent one of a nation’s greatest assets for peace. Investing in education, vocational training, employment, and civic participation gives young people reasons to believe in their future and become stakeholders in stability rather than victims of renewed violence.
Pillars of peace
Strong institutions are equally essential. Peace cannot endure where justice is absent or where citizens lose confidence in public institutions. Liberia’s post-conflict recovery required strengthening democratic governance, public administration, the judiciary, electoral systems, and profession

items.title: Xi Jinping’s AI Vision
items.summary: Xi’s speech addressed the attendees at the World Artificial Intelligence Conference, but his real audience was the international community, and of course the United States.
items.body_text:
Xi Jinping, president of China and general secretary of the Chinese Communist Party (CCP), traveled to Shanghai in mid-July. Of his several missions in Shanghai, none was more important than his opening speech to the World Artificial Intelligence Conference.
Breaking from the norm established since the first World Artificial Intelligence Conference was held in Shanghai in 2018, Xi himself, rather than a leader from the inner circles of the CCP, took the helm on July 17 and opened the conference with his thoughts. And his speech left no doubt that he has decided to take a leading role in the development of AI.
Xi’s speech addressed the attendees at the conference, but his real audience was the international community, and of course the United States, China’s chief competitor in AI development. Surprisingly, Xi began his speech by giving credit to the foreign sources that initiated the study and development of AI.
“Seventy years ago,” Xi told the assembly, “a group of young scholars proposed the concept of artificial intelligence (AI) for the first time at the Dartmouth Workshop in New Hampshire of the United States.”
The reference to the foreign, indeed American, creators who were the progenitors of AI is an uncharacteristic acknowledgement for a Chinese leader to make.
Xi’s nod to Western technology did not end with AI.
“In the course of history,” Xi said, “the invention of the steam engine heralded the industrial civilization, the widespread access to electricity brightened up modern society, and the birth of the internet brought the entire world together.”
All of these inventions originated in Europe or the United States.
While lauding the potential of AI, Xi did not shy away from the reality that much is still unknown about AI’s capabilities:
We human beings must answer the questions posed by our times: How to get along with thinking machines? How to ensure security when algorithm is part of decision-making? How to tackle ethical challenges by technologies through adaptive governance? How to realize AI for all when the divide keeps widening? These questions demand serious consideration and real answers from the whole international community.
One must not forget, however, the world in which Xi Jinping believes. The fundamental question for Xi is: How does a one-party state, which controls and where necessary censors all forms of state-owned and private media alike, all of a sudden take the reins to control a technology that has proven itself to be unpredictable?
Xi alluded to this question. “China lays great emphasis on safety and security in AI development,” he said. “With a deep understanding of the trends and logic of AI development, we are continuously improving laws, regulations, policies, mechanisms, application norms, as well as ethical principles to make sure that AI is safe, secure and controllable, and that this fine steed of AI gallops with both speed and stability.”
It can be surmised that “stability” is the key concept here, as nothing is more precious to the CCP than a stable and content society that continues to carve out space for the party to not only survive, but thrive.
It can be argued that the entire field of AI – handing over control of key systems to a black-box algorithm – is anathema to China’s political model. Perhaps this is the very reason that China is attempting to insert itself as a global leader in AI protocols and standards. The CCP’s top brass certainly realizes that the genie is out of the bottle. AI is here and it is growing in both usage and impact. What happens when AI outflanks and outgrows China’s censors?
Once AI has broken the levees built to keep CCP and government data and information secret, it is difficult to believe that there would not be a backlash from society at large. Therefore, the CCP needs to be able to rein it in, and control AI for its own political safety. items.title: Is Japan Decoupling From China?
items.summary: The new generation of Japanese policymakers is far less willing to accommodate China than its predecessors.
items.body_text:
Japan’s relationship with the People’s Republic of China (PRC) began before formal diplomatic relations were established. Although diplomatic relations were not normalized until 1972, the two countries had already created an unofficial trade mechanism in 1962 that enabled bilateral trade despite the absence of mutual diplomatic recognition.
In a famous article published in Foreign Affairs in 1967, former U.S. Vice President Richard Nixon argued that “we simply cannot afford to leave China forever outside the family of nations.” At the time, Japan’s China policy had already been moving in that direction, going beyond even the policy imagination of its closest ally, the United States.
This was despite intense diplomatic pressure from the United States, which remained firmly anti-communist. Throughout the 1960s, Washington publicly opposed Japan’s efforts to normalize relations with one of its closest neighbors and discouraged any move toward diplomatic recognition of the PRC. The “shock” caused by Nixon’s announcement of his planned visit to mainland China in 1971 stemmed, in part, from Japanese frustration that this policy framework toward China – shaped and constrained by U.S. diplomatic pressure against Japan’s preference – was abruptly reversed without prior consultation with Tokyo.
After normalization, Japan and China entered a honeymoon period in which their relationship resembled a quasi-alliance, rooted in their shared distrust of the Soviet Union as a common adversary. This perception was also shared by the United States, which intensified its pressure against Moscow as Cold War tensions began to rise. From the late 1970s through the 1980s, Japan expanded its industrial assistance to China, while the United States strengthened military cooperation with Beijing, including transfers of military technology. These developments highlight the strategic importance that both Japan and the United States placed on their relationship with China.
A turning point in China-Japan relations came on June 4, 1989, when the People’s Liberation Army moved into Tiananmen Square to suppress student protesters. Images of the violence were broadcast around the world, prompting the U.S.-led Western bloc to impose sanctions in response to China’s violent crackdown.
Although Japan suspended its aid program to China, it was reluctant to fully participate in broader sanctions. It was Japan, at the critical G7 summit in Paris, that took the lead in preventing China’s complete isolation from the international community. Its efforts resulted in the inclusion of the following sentence in the summit declaration: “We look to the Chinese authorities to create conditions which will avoid their isolation and provide for a return to cooperation based upon the resumption of movement towards political and economic reform, and openness.” At that critical juncture, Japan was prepared to break with the emerging Western consensus in order to prevent China from being pushed back into international isolation.
The history reviewed above is essential for understanding the current state of China-Japan relations. Since the 1960s, the two nations have consistently maintained some level of economic exchange despite the political circumstances of each period. The characterization of their relationship as “hot economics and cold politics” has been a defining feature of bilateral ties, particularly over the past several decades. During the 1980s, and especially in the aftermath of the Tiananmen Incident, a strategic dimension also helped sustain the partnership, as both countries continued to view their relationship through the lens of shared geopolitical interests.
However, when examining the China-Japan relationship today, it may be more accurately described as one of “cooling economics and colder politics” – a trajectory that relations had not previously taken.

items.title: Uzbekistan’s Nuclear Power Plant Project Advances
items.summary: Officials say that the first small modular reactor of Uzbekistan’s nuclear power plant project is to be commissioned in 2029.
items.body_text:
The head of Uzatom, Uzbekistan’s atomic energy agency, Azim Akhmedkhadjayev said recently that the first small modular reactor of Uzbekistan’s ongoing nuclear power plant (NPP) project is to be commissioned in 2029, while the first large reactor will come online in 2033. The project itself will be completed in 2034-2035. The NPP will produce up to 17 billion kWh of electricity per year, which, according to Akhmedkhadjayev, will amount to 20 percent of the country’s energy production. Current annual production volume is 80 billion kWh.
Having an NPP is not a new dream for Uzbekistan. The first president of the country, Islam Karimov, also understood the need for a nuclear power plant, but never took concrete steps toward its realization. Shavkat Mirziyoyev, however, did not waste any time. In December 2017, just a year after Mirziyoyev came to power, Tashkent and Rosatom, the Russian state nuclear energy corporation, agreed to build a two-reactor NPP in Uzbekistan.
In 2019, Tashkent adopted a law “On the Use of Atomic Energy for Peaceful Purposes,” outlining a legal framework that includes state ownership rules, safety protocols, and so on. In 2024, Uzatom was established as an authorized body to implement state policy under the Cabinet of Ministers, replacing the Agency for the Development of Atomic Energy that had existed under the Ministry of Energy.
After years of negotiation and consideration of several different options, in September 2025, Uzbekistan and Rosatom finally signed an agreement to build an integrated nuclear power plant in Jizzakh with two small modular reactors (SMRs), specifically RITM-200N reactors, with a capacity of 55 megawatts each, and two large VVER-1000 reactors, each generating 1 GW. Russian President Vladimir Putin and Uzbekistan’s Mirziyoyev officially launched the construction of the plant in June this year at a ceremony held in Saint Petersburg.
The project was initially estimated to cost $10-13 billion; however, last month, Uzatom’s Akhmadkhodjayev said that the expected cost is $9.5 billion at most. Even this figure is arguably too big for Uzbekistan, whose external debt is already over $82 billion as of early 2026. Tashkent plans to attract around 85-90 percent of the NPP construction funds in the form of loans from diverse sources, hoping it will return over $165 billion to the state budget.
Tashkent has been trying to present the project as multilaterally financed; a project free from Russian loans.
“We are not currently considering Russian money, given all the geopolitical developments,” said Akhmadkhodjayev in March 2025. At the time, the project under consideration consisted of six small modular reactors, which were estimated to have a price tag of just $2 billion. He argued that the construction of the plant would not place Uzbekistan in a debt trap despite most of the money being planned to be borrowed from external actors.
“They [investors, lenders] will receive the profits generated by the nuclear power plant in the form of dividends. They will not have any involvement in the management [of the plant]. This is stupid,” explained Akhmadkhodjayev.
Half a year later, after the project had been revised to its final form — consisting of two small modular reactors and two large capacity reactors — the head of the directorate for the construction of nuclear power plants in Uzbekistan, Abdujamil Qalmuratov, voiced a different cost: $1 billion for the small reactors. He said that the money will come from the state budget.
“Yes, it’s the state budget. The state is building it — it’s a completely Uzbek project. The source of funding is our budget. The nuclear project must be national,” reinstated Qalmuratov.

items.title: With America deranged, President Xi summons overseas Chinese
items.summary: 就让岁月开成一朵花， 等一场春风温柔抵达， 带着知足上路， 带着晚霞回家， 爱在时光中轻轻发芽。 – 吴忧 And so it begins. President Xi Jinping of China has summoned overseas Chinese to pool strengths and contribute to the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. This is not new. The People’s Republic of China has frequently called on the 60 million-strong Chinese diaspora to help the motherland, with periodic […] The post With America deranged, President Xi summons overseas Chinese appeared first on Asia Times.
items.body_text:
就让岁月开成一朵花，
等一场春风温柔抵达，
带着知足上路，
带着晚霞回家，
爱在时光中轻轻发芽。
– 吴忧
And so it begins.
President Xi Jinping of China has summoned overseas Chinese to pool strengths and contribute to the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. This is not new. The People’s Republic of China has frequently called on the 60 million-strong Chinese diaspora to help the motherland, with periodic pronouncements seeking cultural ties, technical expertise and commercial opportunities all couched in aiding the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation.
Most famously, 600,000 overseas Chinese heeded the call and returned from Southeast Asia after the People’s Republic was established in 1949. The grandfather of yours truly was among them, founding schools in Fujian province.
At the National Committee of the People’s Political Consultative Conference (NCPPCC) meeting in Beijing on July 27 and 28, a session on overseas Chinese affairs was held for the first time since party and state institutions were overhauled in 2018 – a point that was specifically highlighted by the pronouncement.
The pronouncement, released on July 29, includes one stunning element: President Xi Jinping has called on overseas Chinese “to leverage their unique strengths in support of the cause of national reunification.”
“National reunification,” said the Global Times (a nationalist newspaper). I had to reread it a couple times. Was it a typo? Surely they meant “national rejuvenation,” right? Who’s against rejuvenation?
In the official Chinese language announcement on the NCPPCC website, President Xi urged “sons and daughters of China at home and abroad to unite and strive (海内外中华儿女团结奋斗)” to achieve a “united and unified Chinese nation, the ‘root’ of Chinese people at home and abroad.”
President Xi Jinping of China has indeed requested the Chinese diaspora to lend our unique strengths towards national reunification. Overseas Chinese will do rejuvenation all day long, but, c’mon, reunification? What is President Xi asking, exactly?
National reunification with Taiwan under the People’s Republic of China is politically anathema in the West, especially the US – ignorantly so, but still. Many, if not most, long established overseas Chinese in America would just as well kick this can down the road for as many decades as possible, hoping events do not outrun their IBGYBG strategy (I’ll be gone, you’ll be gone).
These overseas Chinese have it good in America – respectable careers, spacious homes, children in elite schools, citizenship and excellent fishing. This is the American dream as promised, is it not?
Of late, however, we all sense things have gone awry. This, of course, is not a concern unique to overseas Chinese. It is a common lament in America. As public discourse is captured by deranged culture wars, politics has become gratuitously divisive and the media have become a free-for-all of disinformation and low-wattage slop.
Many overseas China wonder, often secretly, whether they (or their parents) made the right decision decades ago after jumping for joy on receiving US graduate school acceptances. They were at the top of their TPFSZUN (Tsinghua, Peking, Fudan, Shanghai Jiaotong, Zhejiang, USTC and Nanjing) class in physics, chemistry and engineering. A PhD program in America was the obvious next step, one which nobody turned down.
And now they can’t help but wonder. Many are professors or middle managers in the research departments of Fortune 500 companies. It’s fine, they tell themselves. They achieved the American dream. It’s all for the next generation, anyway, and the next generation has clocked +1550 on the SATs, plays the oboe, started a bogus charity, took up a ridiculous sport like squash and is on track to the Ivy League.
Some of them, at least. A few crashed out spectacularly after getting sucked in by some bizarro American subculture – skater, stoner, hip-hop, goth, non-binary. Of course, these are the odd cases. Much more common is the +1550 SAT, cellist, bogus charity founder and fencing medalist

items.title: South Korea: the ‘model ally’?
items.summary: US Undersecretary of War Elbridge Colby called South Korea (Republic of Korea, ROK) a “model ally” while visiting Seoul a few months ago. A “model ally?” Compared with what? South Korea is still a longtime partner and an ally bound by a mutual defense treaty signed in 1953. However, all relationships change over time, and the US-ROK relationship isn’t […] The post South Korea: the ‘model ally’? appeared first on Asia Times.
items.body_text:
US Undersecretary of War Elbridge Colby called South Korea (Republic of Korea, ROK) a “model ally” while visiting Seoul a few months ago. A “model ally?” Compared with what?
South Korea is still a longtime partner and an ally bound by a mutual defense treaty signed in 1953. However, all relationships change over time, and the US-ROK relationship isn’t what it once was.
Most of America’s “model” allies don’t have influential figures associated with the ruling party – in this case, the elder brother of Kim Min-Seok, until recently the prime minister and now in the running to head the ruling Democratic Party of Korea (DPK) – who have declared that Trump’s America is “the apex of Yankee imperialism.”
It’s equally difficult to find an equivalent in other US alliances of the rare circumstances that the former prime minister himself and the head of the ruling party, were both imprisoned as younger men for pro-North Korea acts against the US ambassador’s residence and a US Information Agency office in South Korea. Neither has ever apologized or even explained it away as “youthful exuberance.”
And South Korea’s President himself, Lee Jae Myung, has referred to US forces in South Korea after World War II as an “occupying force.” He was also accused of being involved in the unauthorized transfer of US$8 million to North Korea while serving as governor of Gyeonggi Province. Lee denies the charges, but his then-subordinate has been convicted.
Since taking office in mid-2025, the Lee administration’s Unification Ministry has seemed keen to provoke the United States. The South Korean government early on picked a fight over longstanding, effective bilateral procedures for managing the Demilitarized Zone between South and North Korea.
South Korean prosecutors also improperly accessed restricted areas (and reportedly, sensstive information) at Osan Air Base while pursuing an investigation into activities by the former South Korean administration directed at North Korea. On another occasion, a Lee administration official released secret information on North Korean nuclear activities provided by the US.
Other South Korean officials are pushing to assume wartime “operational control” over combined ROK and US forces more for political reasons than on the basis of meeting actual readiness requirements – and contrary to bilateral understandings on when such changes will be made.
Chafing US global policies
“Model ally” South Korea has not been helpful with the US campaign against Iran, and has complained about modest transfers of US military hardware from South Korea to the Middle East.
The Lee administration doesn’t seem interested in helping out with the defense of Taiwan either, which is the lynchpin of the US defense line in the Indo-Pacific and of great importance to South Korea’s own security. Nor is it keen to give US forces in South Korea permission to redeploy in the event of a Taiwan contingency. This perhaps isn’t surprising. While a candidate for the presidency, Lee Jae Myung said Taiwan was none of South Korea’s business, a stance that is music to Beijing’s ears.
President Lee Jae Myung’s recent social media postings include comments equating Israeli military actions with the Holocaust, provoking a formal complaint from the Israeli government. Lee offered a half-hearted, incoherent excuse.
And the South Korean administration sent $500,000 to Iran for ‘humanitarian aid’ – but how likely is this to help families of the several tens of thousands of Iranians the regime gunned down a few months ago for demanding honest, consensual government? Not likely at all, and Lee didn’t even appear to pay lip service to the idea.
A one-party ‘model ally’?
And there’s more that makes one wonder about the definition of “model ally.”

items.title: China exit rules tightened to guard rare earth, battery secrets
items.summary: China will tighten its exit-entry rules from September 15 to stop experienced engineers from leaking knowhow in industries subject to export controls and deter tourists from visiting “high-risk” nations such as Japan. The State Council’s new regulation, which spans 19 articles and was announced on July 31, sets up a coordinated system to warn citizens […] The post China exit rules tightened to guard rare earth, battery secrets appeared first on Asia Times.
items.body_text:
China will tighten its exit-entry rules from September 15 to stop experienced engineers from leaking knowhow in industries subject to export controls and deter tourists from visiting “high-risk” nations such as Japan.
The State Council’s new regulation, which spans 19 articles and was announced on July 31, sets up a coordinated system to warn citizens of overseas risks, verify the purpose of each exit-entry application and tighten restrictions on both citizens and foreigners.
The regulation states that:
- immigration and visa authorities can question applicants and demand documents or data to verify identity and travel purpose, and invitation letter issuers are liable for their authenticity;
- citizens violating export control or technology trade rules or those who may endanger national industrial or technological security will be barred from leaving by commerce departments;
- when processing travel documents and border checks, authorities must remind citizens headed to high-risk countries to travel cautiously, and may discourage travel to destinations under the highest-level warning;
- those committing crimes abroad that harm national security face bans of six months to three years after returning (uthorities barring someone from leaving must notify immigration agencies and inform the person in writing of the facts, reasons and appeal channels, except where it could affect national security or a criminal probe);
- agencies providing exit-entry intermediary services must register with local immigration authorities within 15 days of setup, with staff registered by their employers, and existing agencies must register within 90 days.
The export control clause does not name specific sectors, but Chinese commentators said it targets fields where Beijing has already imposed its own restrictions, including electric vehicle (EV) batteries, solar panels and rare earths.
“There are many situations that could endanger national security and interests, and it is hard to spell out every one of them in legislation,” said Cheng Xiezhong, a legal scholar and professor at the China University of Political Science and Law. “The new regulation names one such situation, which is the violation of export control or technology trade management.”
He says unauthorized exports of dual-use items or transferring key industrial technology abroad will fall under the provision of “causing harm to national security and interests” in Article 12 of the new exit-entry law.
“‘May endanger’ is one of the key phrasings in the regulation,” says a Shandong-based columnist writing under the pen name “Xinghe Duke.”
“It means the authorities won’t wait until harm is done, but they will take precautionary measures. The wording of ‘Decided by the commerce authority and other departments’ means there is a lawful process. ‘Barred from leaving’ does not mean arrest; it just means the targeted person cannot leave the country.”
He says that the State Council’s Regulations on Overseas Investment, which took effect July 1, bars investors from moving export control goods, technology, services or data abroad by sending staff, arranging overseas work, giving technical guidance or running cross-border training. He adds that engineers who have the know-how in core technologies such as electrolyte formulas, N-type solar cell technology and rare earth separation are the main targets.
 
“In the past, foreign companies dodged China’s export controls by poaching Chinese engineers, offering them higher pay, green cards and equity to help build identical factories in Vietnam, India or Mexico,” he says. “That path is now closed under the new regulation.”
He adds that the United States and Japanese rare earth separation projects in Australia and Texas have relied on Chinese talent to break purity bottlenecks.

items.title: Cuba encadena dos apagones nacionales en menos de 24 horas y no logra levantar la red eléctrica
items.summary: La red eléctrica cubana volvió a colapsar este lunes 3 de agosto cuando el Gobierno intentaba restablecerla tras el apagón general del domingo por la noche. Es el sexto corte nacional del año y el undécimo en dos años de una crisis que arrastran las termoeléctricas construidas en los años sesenta y el bloqueo petrolero estadounidense, que dejó a la isla casi sin crudo desde enero. En La Habana los cortes diarios superan las veinte horas y el malestar se expresa en cacerolazos.

items.title: Armando Vargas: "Aunque la tasa de homicidios cayó en México, los casos siguen siendo altos"
items.summary: México cerró 2025 con la mayor caída de homicidios en más de una década. Según el Instituto Nacional de Estadística y Geografía, el país registró 27.989 presuntos homicidios el año pasado, 5.561 menos que en 2024, una reducción del 16,6 %. Con esta baja, la tasa nacional pasó de 25,8 a 21,4 homicidios por cada 100.000 habitantes, su nivel más bajo desde 2016. Lo analizamos con Armando Vargas, académico, analista y coordinador del Programa de Seguridad de México Evalúa.

items.title: Morocco honors Trump with name change
items.summary: Morocco has named a major highway after US President Donald Trump in recognition of his support for Rabat’s Western Sahara policy Read Full Article at RT.com
items.body_text:
Morocco honors Trump with name change
Morocco has named one of its largest road projects after US President Donald Trump, describing the gesture as an expression of “deep appreciation” for his role in strengthening relations between Washington and Rabat.
King Mohammed VI informed Trump in a letter reported by the state-run Moroccan News Agency (MAP) on Sunday that the 1,055km Tiznit-Dakhla Expressway would be renamed the “Donald J. Trump Highway.”
The monarch said that bilateral relations, traditionally rooted in friendship and loyalty, have become particularly “vibrant and fruitful” during Trump’s two presidential terms.
”Your historic recognition, in 2020, of Morocco’s sovereignty over its Sahara will forever be etched in the memory of Moroccans, from one generation to the next,” the king wrote in a previously undisclosed letter dated July 2.
Trump thanked the monarch in a July 26 post on his Truth Social platform, describing the decision as a “great honor” and expressing hope that he would travel the highway’s entire length.
The road connects Tiznit in southern Morocco with Dakhla in the disputed Western Sahara region, passing through Guelmim and Laayoune along the Atlantic coast.
Rabat considers Western Sahara part of its territory and took control of most of the former Spanish colony after Spain withdrew in 1975. The Algeria-backed Polisario Front seeks to establish an independent Sahrawi state. A UN-brokered ceasefire took effect in 1991, but efforts to hold a referendum on the territory’s status have stalled.
Morocco submitted an autonomy proposal for Western Sahara to the UN Security Council in April 2007. Under the plan, local authorities would exercise executive, legislative, and judicial powers, while the territory would retain the Moroccan flag and currency. Rabat would remain responsible for foreign policy, national security, and defense.
The US became the first country to formally recognize Moroccan sovereignty over Western Sahara during Trump’s first term in 2020. Washington has maintained that position, with Trump recently reiterating support for Morocco’s autonomy proposal as the only basis for resolving the dispute.
Morocco is considered one of America’s oldest allies and its longest-standing partner in Africa. Rabat says it became the first country to recognize US independence in 1777. The two countries signed a Treaty of Peace and Friendship in 1786, establishing what Washington describes as its longest unbroken treaty relationship.
The US designated Morocco a major non-NATO ally in 2004. A bilateral free-trade agreement took effect two years later, making Morocco the only African country with such an accord with Washington. US exports to Morocco reached $5.5 billion in 2025, according to the Office of the US Trade Representative.
Morocco also hosts African Lion, the US Africa Command’s largest annual military exercise on the continent.
The close relationship has also featured in speculations surrounding the recent mass migrant crossings from Morocco into the Spanish enclave of Ceuta. El País reported that some members of Spain’s governing coalition suspected that the crisis may have been orchestrated by Rabat with US and Israeli support to pressure Madrid over its foreign policy, including its opposition to military action against Iran. Neither Washington nor Rabat has responded directly to the allegation.
The decision to rename the highway has drawn criticism from Western Sahara Resource Watch, an advocacy group that describes the disputed territory as “Africa’s last colony.” Its representative Roberto Cantoni told Spanish newspaper El Independiente that the renaming was intended “not to promote trade with the US, but to inflate the president’s ego.”
Algeria, which supports the Polisario Front and rejects Rabat’s proposal to grant Western Sahara autonomy under Moroccan sovereignty, has not officially responded to the highway’s naming. However, Algerian daily El Watan accused Morocco of “selling off its di

items.summary: Armed men have killed 12 people, abducted women and children, and stolen livestock during an overnight raid in Nigeria’s Sokoto State Read Full Article at RT.com
items.body_text:
Gunmen kill 12 and abduct women and children in northwest Nigeria
At least 12 people have been killed and an unspecified number of women and children abducted in an attack by gunmen in northwestern Nigeria, Reuters has reported, citing local residents.
Armed men, as yet unidentified by the authorities, entered the village of Lajinge in Sokoto State at around 11 PM local time on Saturday and attacked residents until approximately 3 AM on Sunday.
Six members of one family were killed when their home was set on fire, according to witnesses. “They killed at least 12 people, injured four others, abducted women and children after rustling many livestock,” resident Auwal Hassan told Reuters by telephone.
Sokoto police spokesperson Ahmed Rufai also told the outlet that an investigation had been launched and that the force would provide further information later. No group has claimed responsibility for the attack.
The northwest region of Africa’s most populous nation has faced persistent attacks by heavily armed gangs commonly known as bandits. The groups raid rural communities, kidnap residents for ransom, steal livestock, and demand payments from farmers seeking access to their land.
Nigeria has also experienced an upsurge in mass abductions amid a worsening security crisis, despite President Bola Tinubu declaring a nationwide security emergency in November and ordering the recruitment of thousands of additional police officers and military personnel. Boko Haram, Islamic State West Africa Province and the Al-Qaeda-linked Ansaru group have been blamed for attacks on villages, churches, and schools, as well as mass kidnappings.
On May 15, gunmen seized 39 pupils and seven teachers from three schools in Oyo State. The authorities said 44 surviving captives were freed on July 10 following a military operation. Last November, 25 Muslim schoolgirls were abducted from a government school in Kebbi State, while about 230 children and teachers were seized days later from a Catholic school in neighboring Niger State. All were subsequently freed, according to the authorities. Last month, the government announced an expanded Safe Schools framework involving fencing, lighting, security personnel, and monitoring technology as part of measures to address the crisis.
On Sunday, the Nigerian Army said troops foiled an attempted “infiltration” of a military base in Zamfara State by terrorists. An army officer and a police officer were killed, while nine of an unspecified number of abducted civilians were rescued, the military said in a statement.

The US deployed around 200 troops to Nigeria in February for training and technical support after conducting joint airstrikes with Nigerian forces in December. Most have since been withdrawn, although Washington continues intelligence sharing and wider security cooperation with Abuja, according to the US Africa Command.
The deployment followed the withdrawal of French and US forces from parts of the wider Sahel, which reduced Western intelligence and military capabilities as armed groups expanded across the region.

items.title: DR Congo facing largest ever Ebola outbreak – WHO
items.summary: DR Congo is facing its biggest Ebola outbreak ever with 49 health zones affected, the WHO says Read Full Article at RT.com
items.body_text:
DR Congo facing largest ever Ebola outbreak – WHO
The Ebola outbreak currently spreading through the Democratic Republic of Congo (DR Congo) is the largest the country has ever faced, the World Health Organization (WHO) said on Saturday.
Infections are spreading despite months of response efforts, according to the agency. The current outbreak, DR Congo’s 17th, has reportedly surpassed the country’s 2018-2020 Ebola epidemic to become the largest on record.
The currently untreatable Bundibugyo virus, for which there are no approved vaccines, was initially detected in the Mongbwalu health zone in Ituri Province, but has spread across five provinces in two months and now affects 49 health zones, the agency noted. The affected provinces are Ituri, North Kivu, South Kivu, Haut-Uele, and Tshopo.
The outbreak is “intensifying, with sustained transmission and continued increases in reported cases and deaths,” the WHO stated.
During epidemiological week 30, the country recorded a weekly record of 567 new cases and 296 deaths, the highest figures since the outbreak began.
The latest Congolese Ministry of Health data put the number of confirmed cases at 3,674, up from the 3,605 reported by the WHO as of July 30. The death toll has climbed to 1,621, while 760 patients remain in isolation or are hospitalized and 666 people have recovered. The overall case fatality rate stands at 44.1%.
The agency said insecurity, mass displacement, population movements, and cross-border travel are hampering containment efforts and raising the risk of further spread. Despite those challenges, the Congolese Health Ministry said surveillance systems and laboratory testing remain operational, while contact tracing has improved, although it remains below target. The nationwide contact follow-up rate currently stands at 78%.
WHO said a substantial scaling up of the response involving the Congolese authorities, the UN agency, and international partners will be needed to bring the outbreak under control.
Elsewhere in the region, Uganda declared its Bundibugyo Ebola outbreak over on July 28 after going 42 days without recording a locally transmitted case. However, WHO warned that the country remains at risk of imported infections as transmission continues in neighboring DR Congo.

items.title: Organizers unveil hymn for Seoul WYD
items.summary: With just one year to go before 2027 World Youth Day in Seoul, its official theme song is announced: Confidite, Ego Vici Mundum, or “Take courage! I have overcome the world”. Read all
items.body_text:
Organizers unveil hymn for Seoul WYD
By Cécile Mérieux
It is a tune that will echo the minds of an entire generation of young Catholics. The official theme song for the next World Youth Day (WYD) has been unveiled, exactly one year ahead of the event. The hymn will set the tone for this upcoming international gathering of Catholic youth, who will gather in Seoul from August 3 to 8, 2027.
An hymn for all nations
The theme song is entitled Confidite, Ego Vici Mundum and takes up the theme chosen for WYD 2027: âTake courage! I have overcome the world,â a verse from Johnâs Gospel (16:33). An international hymn, the song is performed in several languages, including Korean, English, French, Spanish, Portuguese, and Italian.
The song opens with this invitation: âCome follow me, sleeping heart, wake up and walkâ. Two versions have been recorded, the first (which can be seen at the top of this article) in a more classical style, featuring a choir and orchestra, while the second is a remixed pop version (which you can view at the bottom).
Singing of communion
One aim of this song is to offer a foretaste of the event. Above all, however, it will serve as the permanent soundtrack for participants as they prepare for the gathering. Each edition has its corresponding melody, carrying with it a wealth of memories for the participants.
The hymn is the result of an open contest. The task was to create an original composition that translated the WYD theme, âTake courage! I have overcome the worldâ (Jn 16:33). The initiative was a success, drawing 434 submissions, including 294 from abroad. The selected song was then submitted for approval to the Holy Seeâs Dicastery for Laity, Family and Life.
A Korean WYD
The theme song was composed by Korean musician Francis Jiyoon Kim, who gave it the flavor of his country and culture. Sung largely in Korean, the vocals blend with local traditional instruments in a contemporary arrangement. The music video showcases the landscapes and iconic sights of Seoul, offering a first glimpse of what awaits participants next summer.
As is tradition, the âDays in the Diocesesâ will precede the main gathering in the capital. From July 29 to August 2, 2027, fifteen Korean dioceses will welcome pilgrims into parishes and families, offering them an immersion into the life of the local Church prior to the celebrations in Seoul.
More than thirty years after Manila in 1995, this WYD will be only the second held in Asia. It marks the first time the event has been hosted in a country where Catholics are a minority. In South Korea, Catholics represent roughly 12% of the population, in a society marked by significant religious pluralism.
Next steps
Pilgrim registrations will open in October 2026, offering various packages based on the length of stay and selected events. A mobile app and an integrated logistics system are also being developed.
As in previous editions, hospitality will largely be provided by families and parishes across the Archdiocese of Seoul. Around 230 parishes are already actively recruiting and training host families so that young people can experience the daily life of the Korean Church.
âWe will make every effort to ensure that WYD Seoul 2027 is a celebration of hope and a testament to the hospitality and solidarity of Korea and Seoul,â said Archbishop Peter Chung Soon-taick, Archbishop of the Archdiocese of Seoul and President of the Local Organizing Committee. Teams have been preparing the event for three years now, and they are now entering the home stretch before welcoming hundreds of thousands of young people from around the world. Nearly 30,000 volunteers are expected to be mobilized, with several hundred already at work.

items.title: A century of Trinitarian mission in Madagascar full of hope, freedom and mercy
items.summary: The Order of the Most Holy Trinity and of the Captives mark a century of missionary presence in Madagascar, it gives thanks for generations of missionaries whose service has strengthened the local Church, fostered vocations, and carried the Gospel to the country’s most remote communities. The centenary also renews the order’s commitment to bring hope and redemption to the new frontiers of today's world. Read all
items.body_text:
A century of Trinitarian mission in Madagascar full of hope, freedom and mercy
By Sr. Christine Masivo, CPS
The Order of the Most Holy Trinity and of the Captives, also known as the Trinitarians, is celebrating 100 years of missionary presence in Madagascar, commemorating a century of evangelization, pastoral service, and witness to the Gospel that has profoundly shaped both the local Church and the Trinitarian Order.
A century of missionary witness
The anniversary recalls the departure of the first five Trinitarian missionaries from Rome on June 4, 1926, shortly after the Solemnity of the Most Holy Trinity. Accompanied by the then Minister General, Fr. Francis Xavier of the Immaculate Conception, they set out to establish the Trinitarian mission in Madagascar after the order withdrew from Somalia in 1924. They learned the Malagasy and French languages before settling in Miarinarivo, the mission territory entrusted to them.
Reflecting on the centenary, the Minister General, Fr. Luigi Buccarello, told the Vatican's Fides news agency, that the first missionaries demonstrated "the evangelical courage" to cross cultural, linguistic, and religious borders in response to the Holy Spirit's promptings. Their journey, he noted, was not merely an expansion of the Order but an expression of its enduring missionary identity.
An apostolate of evangelization and human dignity
Inspired by the charism of St. John de Matha and St. Felix of Valois, the Trinitarian mission has always united the proclamation of the Gospel with the defense of human freedom and dignity. Founded during a period marked by conflict and slavery, the Order originally dedicated itself to aiding captives, a mission that continues today through service to those living on the margins of society.
In Madagascar, the missionaries centered their apostolate on extensive pastoral visits to remote villages, ensuring that scattered Christian communities remained connected to the life of the Church, which they invested in the formation of catechists and pastoral workers through a Catechetical Formation Centre, equipping local leaders for evangelization. At the same time, they built churches, schools, and multipurpose centers while restoring places of worship to support both spiritual and social development.
Throughout their ministry, the Trinitarians sought to respect local cultures and traditions while accompanying communities in faith. Their work contributed not only to evangelization but also to education, pastoral formation, and the strengthening of Christian communities across the island.
Flourishing mission to the future
The Trinitarian mission in Madagascar has grown remarkably over the past century, fulfilling its goal of building self-sustaining local churches. Beginning with the establishment of the Apostolic Vicariate of Miarinarivo in 1939, the first ecclesiastical territory in Africa entrusted to the Order, the mission later expanded to Tsiroanomandidy and Ambatondrazaka.
Today, the Trinitarians serve in twelve of Madagascar's twenty-two dioceses, with flourishing local vocations, missionaries serving abroad, and five Trinitarian bishops emerging from the Malagasy Church.
Marking the centenary, Fr. Buccarello described the anniversary as a call to renew the Order's missionary commitment, especially to the cultural, social, and spiritual frontiers of today's world. As the Trinitarians give thanks for generations of missionaries who served with dedication and sacrifice, they celebrate a century in which a small missionary presence has grown into a vibrant Church that continues to proclaim the Gospel as a sign of hope, freedom, and mercy.

items.title: Catholic Sisters in the Legal Profession called to prophetic witness
items.summary: Around 200 participants gathered for the first Catholic Sisters in the Legal Profession Network Conference in Nairobi, Kenya. Among them are canon lawyers, civil lawyers, major superiors, safeguarding professionals, researchers, and other Church leaders. Under the theme, "Prophetic Witness, Safeguarding as an Expression of the Gospel," participants reflected on strengthening safeguarding, justice, and accountability in religious life. Read all
items.body_text:
Catholic Sisters in the Legal Profession called to prophetic witness
Sr. Christine Masivo, CPS â Vatican City
The conference provided an opportunity for participants to reflect on the prophetic role of legal professionals in promoting safeguarding, justice, and accountability within religious life.
Prophetic witness
Delivering the keynote address, Sr. Jane Wakahiu, LSOSF, the Associate Vice President of Programme Operations and Head of Catholic Sisters at the Conrad N. Hilton Foundation, welcomed participants and expressed appreciation for the efforts invested in organising the gathering. She described the conference as a meaningful sign of hope and a shared commitment to strengthening religious life in Africa through dialogue, collaboration, and service.
Reflecting on the conference theme, "Prophetic Witness: Safeguarding as an Expression of the Gospel," Sr. Wakahiu explained that prophetic witness is rooted in faithful living of Gospel values. It means standing in solidarity with those who suffer, speaking the truth with love, and challenging injustice through God's mercy, compassion, and justice.
Upholding the dignity of all
The keynote address emphasised that safeguarding is not simply an administrative requirement or a legal obligation but a Gospel imperative flowing directly from Christ's command to love one's neighbour.
Sr Wakahiu further challenged religious institutes and ecclesial communities to examine assumptions and practices that diminish the dignity of women, children, and vulnerable adults. Referring to the Pontifical Commission for the Protection of Minors' 2024 report, she highlighted safeguarding challenges affecting many African contexts, including weak national guidelines, limited survivor accompaniment, insufficient safeguarding professionals, inadequate resources, and gaps in accountability.
The conference, she said, provided an opportunity to strengthen awareness, develop safeguarding procedures, and accompany survivors more effectively within Church communities.
